lead: The lame man healed at the Beautiful Gate is now clinging to Peter and John, and a crowd gathers. Peter turns the astonishment into a sermon: the power is not ours, it is the name of the Jesus whom God has raised. In the Gospel the two disciples from Emmaus are still telling their story when Jesus himself stands among the eleven, shows his hands and feet, eats before them, and opens their minds to the Scriptures. Psalm 8 marvels that God crowns a mortal with glory and honour, and Easter shows how far that crowning goes.
Both readings turn on the same word: witnesses. Peter says, “To this we are witnesses”, and Jesus says, “You are witnesses of these things.” The key words today are name, Scripture and witness.

r.h: The Author of life, whom God raised
set: This is Peter's second sermon in Acts. A man lame from birth has just been healed at the gate of the Temple (3:1–10). The crowd runs to Solomon's Portico, the covered colonnade along the east side of the Temple court, where Jesus himself once walked and taught (John 10:23). Peter speaks to fellow Israelites as one of them: “the God of our ancestors”.

The sermon is full of old titles for Jesus: servant, Holy and Righteous One, Author of life, Messiah, the prophet like Moses. Luke gathers them to show that the Resurrection does not replace Israel's Scriptures. It opens them.
str: vv. 11–12: the crowd stares; not by our own power or piety.
vv. 13–16: God has glorified his servant; you rejected him, God raised him; his name has healed this man.
vv. 17–18: you acted in ignorance; God fulfilled what the prophets foretold.
vv. 19–21: repent and turn; times of refreshing; the Messiah kept in heaven until the restoration.
vv. 22–26: Moses, Samuel and the prophets; the blessing promised to Abraham, sent first to you.
kw: The word used for the Servant of the Lord in the Greek of Isaiah 52:13: “my servant shall prosper; he shall be exalted and lifted up”. Peter points to the suffering servant who is raised.
Archēgos is the one who leads the way and begins something: a pioneer, a founder. The contrast is sharp: they asked for a murderer, a taker of life, and rejected the one from whom life comes.

“The time of universal restoration” is the final renewal of all things that the prophets promised, when Christ comes again. It does not mean that everyone is automatically saved, an idea later linked with Origen that the Church did not accept.
vv: as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk?
The first thing Peter does is to step out of the way. A minister of Christ points beyond himself.
and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses.
The whole Easter faith in a single verse: what people did, what God did, and the apostles' task. The life that was killed could not stay dead.
“And now, friends, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers.
Peter does not condemn his hearers. He calls them friends and offers them a way back, as Jesus prayed from the Cross, “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).
When God raised up his servant, he sent him first to you, to bless you by turning each of you from your wicked ways.”
The sermon ends with blessing, not threat. The promise to Abraham has not been withdrawn from his children. It is offered to them first.
ch: The Catechism cites this very passage when it teaches that neither all Jews of Jesus' time nor Jews today may be held responsible for his death, and it takes up Peter's words about ignorance (CCC 597). It adds that all sinners were the authors of Christ's Passion (CCC 598). The Second Vatican Council says the same in Nostra Aetate 4. Peter's sermon is a model for preaching: it tells the truth about sin, puts God's action in the centre, and ends with an open door.

r.h: Touch me and see
set: The two disciples have run back from Emmaus to Jerusalem in the dark. Before they can finish, the eleven tell them that the Lord has appeared to Simon (24:34). Then Jesus himself comes. This is Luke's last great scene before the Ascension, and it gathers all that Luke wants the Church to know about the risen Lord: he is real, he is the same, and he is the key to the Scriptures.
str: v. 35: the Emmaus report: known in the breaking of the bread.
vv. 36–37: “Peace be with you”; they think they see a ghost.
vv. 38–43: hands and feet; flesh and bones; he eats broiled fish.
vv. 44–46: everything written in the law, the prophets and the psalms; he opens their minds.
vv. 47–48: repentance and forgiveness to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem; you are witnesses.
kw: Here it means a disembodied spirit, a phantom. Jesus rules this out at once. The risen body is not a vision.
Jesus shows that he is the same one who was crucified, with his wounds. His body is transformed and glorious, but it is still his body.
The same verb is used of the eyes of the Emmaus disciples (24:31) and of the Scriptures opened to them (24:32). Now he opens their minds. The risen Christ is the one who opens.
vv: Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread.
Two meetings with the Lord stand side by side: in the word on the road and in the breaking of the bread. The Mass has the same two tables.
Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.”
The wounds are his signature. He does not come back with a new identity. The Lord of glory is the one who was nailed.
and he took it and ate in their presence.
He does not need food. He eats to give them proof, and to restore the table fellowship that was broken on Thursday night.
Then he opened their minds to understand the scriptures,

The law, the prophets and the psalms name the three parts of the Hebrew Bible, the psalms standing first among the Writings. Christ is not one topic in Scripture among others. He is the key to the whole.
ch: The Catechism says that the risen Jesus established direct contact with his disciples through touch and the sharing of a meal, to show that he is not a ghost (CCC 645), and that his Resurrection fulfils the promises of the Old Testament and of Jesus himself (CCC 652). It cites this verse when it teaches that Christ must open our minds if Scripture is not to remain a dead letter (CCC 108). The mission in verse 47 is the Church's to this day: to proclaim repentance and forgiveness in his name.

qa: Peter says “you killed the Author of life”. Does this blame the Jewish people?

No. Peter is a Jew speaking to fellow Jews in Jerusalem, and in the same breath he says they acted in ignorance and offers them the blessing first. The Church teaches that the death of Christ cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Each of us, by sin, has a share in why he died (CCC 598).
Why does the risen Jesus eat fish?

To show the disciples that he is not a ghost and that his risen body is real (CCC 645). Luke is answering the doubt that a resurrection is only a spiritual way of speaking. The Church confesses that Christ rose in the same body, now glorified.
rite: During the Octave of Easter every day is celebrated as a solemnity in the Roman Rite: the Gloria is sung, the Sequence Victimae paschali laudes may be used, and the double Alleluia is added to the dismissal. Thursday has long been linked in devotion with the Last Supper, and today's Gospel shows the risen Lord at table with his friends. Families might read the whole of Luke 24 together this evening, Easter as Luke tells it.
study: Peter begins by saying, “not by our own power”. Where do I need to step aside so that Christ is seen?
Peter calls those who rejected Jesus “friends” and offers them blessing. How do I speak to those who have hurt the Church or me?
Jesus shows his wounds to prove who he is. What does that say about my own wounds?
Which part of Scripture do I find hardest to understand, and how might I ask Christ to open it?

lead: Yesterday Peter preached in the Temple. Today he is arrested for it, and stands before the very council that condemned Jesus. Filled with the Holy Spirit, the fisherman who once denied his Lord now declares that there is salvation in no other name. Psalm 118 gives him his text: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.

In the Gospel the same Peter has gone back to his boats in Galilee. After a night of empty nets, a stranger on the shore tells them where to cast, and the beloved disciple cries, “It is the Lord!” Jesus has a charcoal fire ready, with bread and fish. The key words today are name, stone and breakfast: the risen Lord is both the foundation of the Church and the host at her table.

r.h: No other name under heaven
set: The healing of the lame man and Peter's sermon have drawn a crowd, and the Temple authorities step in. Luke names the groups: the priests, the captain of the Temple (the officer in charge of the Temple police), and the Sadducees. The Sadducees were a priestly party who did not accept the resurrection of the dead (compare Luke 20:27; Acts 23:8), so the apostles' preaching troubled them twice over.

The next morning the council meets: rulers, elders and scribes, with Annas and Caiaphas. Annas had been high priest earlier and remained the senior figure of the family; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office from about AD 18 to 36. Nothing certain is known of the John and Alexander named here. This is the first time the apostles stand where Jesus stood.
str: vv. 1–4: arrest at evening; yet about five thousand believe.
vv. 5–7: the council assembles: “By what power or by what name?”
vv. 8–10: Peter, filled with the Spirit: by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth.
v. 11: the rejected stone has become the cornerstone.
v. 12: no other name by which we must be saved.
kw: In the Bible a name stands for the person and his power. The question “by what name?” is the theme of these chapters, and the word appears again and again (3:6, 16; 4:7, 10, 12, 17, 18).
Jesus had promised that when his disciples were brought before rulers, the Holy Spirit would teach them what to say (Luke 12:11–12). Here the promise is kept.

Literally “head of the corner”: the stone that holds two walls together, or the top stone that completes an arch. Psalm 118:22 is quoted of Jesus by Jesus himself (Luke 20:17) and by Peter again in his letter (1 Peter 2:7).
vv: much annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming that in Jesus there is the resurrection of the dead.
The apostles do not only say that Jesus rose. They say that in him the resurrection of the dead has begun. Easter is the first fruits of a harvest.
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders,
A few weeks before, in a courtyard of the high priest's house, a servant girl was enough to make Peter deny Jesus. Now he speaks to the high priest's council itself. The difference is the Spirit.
This Jesus is ‘the stone that was rejected by you, the builders; it has become the cornerstone.’
Peter adds “by you” to the psalm. He applies the verse to the leaders before him, as Jesus did in the parable of the vineyard. The same rejection is the place where God builds.
There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among mortals by which we must be saved.”

The healing of one man's feet becomes a sign of salvation for all. The Greek verb for “healed” in 4:9 is sesōstai, from the same root as “saved” here: bodily healing points to the whole salvation that only Christ gives.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it explains the name of Jesus: the name of the Son of God made man is the only one through which we are saved (CCC 432, 452). The Church holds both truths together. Christ is the one Saviour of all, and those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel, yet seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will, can also attain salvation, always through Christ's grace (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). The declaration Dominus Iesus (2000) restated this teaching for our time.

r.h: It is the Lord!
set: John 20 closed with words that sound like the end of the book (20:30–31). Chapter 21 is an epilogue, and many scholars think it was added by the evangelist's circle, though it is found in every manuscript of the Gospel and belongs to it as Scripture. The scene moves to Galilee, to the lake John calls the Sea of Tiberias, after the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore.

Seven disciples are there. Peter goes back to the work he knew, and the others go with him. Readers have long noticed how much this recalls the first call by the lake in Luke 5:1–11: a night of nothing, a word from Jesus, a great catch.
str: vv. 1–3: seven disciples; “I am going fishing”; a night with nothing.
vv. 4–6: a stranger at daybreak; cast to the right; a net too full to haul.
vv. 7–8: the beloved disciple sees; Peter leaps into the sea.
vv. 9–11: a charcoal fire, fish and bread; one hundred fifty-three large fish; the net is not torn.
vv. 12–14: “Come and have breakfast”; he gives the bread and the fish; the third appearance.
kw: A warm, familiar word, like “lads”. The risen Lord speaks to tired fishermen as a father would.

The word occurs only twice in the New Testament: here, and at the fire in the high priest's courtyard where Peter denied Jesus (18:18). The scene is set for Peter's threefold profession of love that follows (21:15–17).
From the verb that gives schisma, a split. The same root is used of the seamless tunic that was not torn (19:24). Many Fathers saw here the unity of the Church that holds all the nations.
vv: Simon Peter said to them, “I am going fishing.” They said to him, “We will go with you.” They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing.
Night in John is often more than a time of day. Without him the disciples can do nothing (15:5), and their own skill brings up an empty net.
That disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!”
Love sees first; Peter acts first. The beloved disciple recognises, and Peter jumps into the sea. The Church needs both.
So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, a hundred fifty-three of them; and though there were so many, the net was not torn.

St Jerome says that Greek writers on nature counted one hundred fifty-three kinds of fish, so the catch stands for all the nations (in substance). St Augustine notes that 153 is the sum of the numbers from 1 to 17 (in substance). Whatever the number holds, the point is fullness, and Peter is the one who draws the net to Jesus.
Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and did the same with the fish.
The words echo the feeding of the five thousand by this same lake (6:11). The Lord who was their guest at Emmaus is here the host.
ch: The Church has always read this scene as a picture of her mission: the disciples fish, but the catch comes at the Lord's word, and Peter draws the full net ashore. St Augustine, in his homilies on John, contrasts this catch with the first one in Luke 5, where the nets were breaking: there the Church as she now is, with good and bad; here the Church at the end, gathered whole (in substance). The meal of bread and fish, given by the Lord's own hands, has always been heard with the Eucharist in mind.

qa: Does “no other name” mean that all who are not baptized are lost?

No. The Church teaches that all salvation comes through Christ, and also that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel or the Church but seek God sincerely and try to do his will as their conscience shows it can be saved, by grace that comes from Christ (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). This does not lessen the duty of mission; it shows how far Christ's grace reaches (CCC 848).
Why do the disciples not recognise Jesus at first?

In several Easter accounts the risen Lord is not known at once: Mary Magdalene, the Emmaus disciples, the fishermen. His risen body is the same body, yet it is in a new state (CCC 645). He is known when he speaks, when he gives, when he breaks bread. Faith learns to recognise him in the same ways today.
Who were the Sadducees?

A party in Judaism of the time, closely linked with the high-priestly families and the Temple. They accepted the books of Moses as authority and denied the resurrection of the dead, against the Pharisees (Acts 23:8). Many in Israel did not share their views. After the Temple was destroyed in AD 70 they disappear from history.
rite: The Friday of the Easter Octave keeps no fast: it is a solemnity, and the Friday abstinence does not apply on solemnities. The Lectionary for these days moves between Acts and the appearance stories of all four Gospels. In the Roman Rite the Easter candle stands near the ambo or the altar through the whole Easter season, and today's Gospel by the lake at daybreak suits it well: the risen Lord is the light that comes after a night of empty nets.
study: Peter once gave way before a servant girl and now speaks before the council. Where do I need the Spirit's courage?
How do I hold together that Christ is the only Saviour and that God's grace reaches people I do not know?
“That night they caught nothing.” Where have I worked hard without asking the Lord?
Jesus cooks breakfast for tired fishermen. How can I serve those around me in small, practical ways this Easter?

lead: The trial of Peter and John ends without a sentence. The council cannot deny the sign, because the healed man is standing right there, so it forbids them to speak in the name of Jesus. Their answer has been repeated by Christians in every age: we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard. Psalm 118 sings for them: “I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the Lord.”

The Gospel is the summary of Easter in the longer ending of Mark. Twice the news is brought and twice it is not believed, until the Lord himself rebukes the eleven and then, without waiting for them to become perfect, sends them to the whole creation. The weekdays of the Octave end as they began, with witnesses. The key words today are boldness, unbelief and go.

r.h: We cannot keep from speaking
set: This passage continues yesterday's scene before the council. Peter has just declared that there is no other name by which we must be saved. Now Luke shows us the council's reaction, and lets us overhear its private discussion once the apostles have been sent out.

The healed man, more than forty years old (4:22), is the silent centre of the scene. A man lame from birth for forty years was well known at the Temple gate, and nobody can pretend that nothing has happened.
str: v. 13: the council sees boldness in uneducated men, and recognises them as companions of Jesus.
v. 14: the healed man stands beside them; nothing to say.
vv. 15–17: the private debate: we cannot deny it; let us stop it spreading.
v. 18: the order: not to speak or teach in the name of Jesus.
vv. 19–20: the answer: judge whether we should obey you rather than God; we cannot keep silent.
v. 21: more threats, release; the people praise God.
kw: Literally “saying everything”: frank, open speech that does not hide. It becomes a key word of Acts (4:29, 31) and is one of the gifts the Church asks of the Spirit.
Not necessarily unable to read, but without the training of the scribal schools: laymen, not experts in the law. The council is surprised that such men argue from Scripture so well.
Luke calls the healing a “notable sign”. A sign is a miracle seen for its meaning: it points to the power of the risen Jesus.
vv: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John and realized that they were uneducated and ordinary men, they were amazed and recognized them as companions of Jesus.
The best compliment a disciple can receive: that people can tell he has been with Jesus. Their education was the three years at his side.
What will we do with them? For it is obvious to all who live in Jerusalem that a notable sign has been done through them; we cannot deny it.
The council does not dispute the fact. Its question is how to manage it. Truth that cannot be denied can still be avoided.
But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge;

They speak with respect to the lawful authorities of their people and ask them to judge. Yet they are clear that God's command comes first. Peter will say it more briefly in the next chapter: “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (5:29).
for we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”
This is not stubbornness but witness. They speak because of what they have seen. The faith of the Church rests on that seeing.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it teaches that handing on the faith means above all proclaiming Jesus Christ, and that those who have met him cannot keep from speaking (CCC 425). On conscience and authority it teaches that citizens are not bound in conscience to obey civil commands contrary to the moral order or the Gospel, and it cites the apostles' answer “We must obey God rather than men” (CCC 2242). Their response is never violence; it is witness, prayer and patience, as the next scene of Acts shows (4:23–31).

r.h: Go into all the world
set: The oldest Greek manuscripts we have of Mark, the great fourth-century codices Vaticanus and Sinaiticus, end the Gospel at 16:8, with the women running from the tomb in fear. Other manuscripts add this longer ending (16:9–20), which many scholars think was written in the second century by another hand, drawing on the Easter stories of Luke and John. St Irenaeus already quotes it before AD 200 as part of Mark. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture and part of the canonical Gospel, and it is read in the liturgy.
The passage reads like a brief catechism of Easter. Each appearance is told in a sentence or two, and unbelief runs through them all.
str: vv. 9–11: first to Mary Magdalene; she tells the mourners; they do not believe.
vv. 12–13: to two walking into the country; they tell the rest; they do not believe.
v. 14: to the eleven at table; he rebukes their unbelief and hardness of heart.
v. 15: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.”
kw: The word runs through the passage like a refrain (vv. 11, 13, 14). The first witnesses of the Resurrection were not credulous people. They had to be overcome by the evidence.
A biblical word for the refusal to let God's word in. Mark has spoken of the disciples' hardened hearts before (6:52; 8:17).
Not only to every nation but to all creation. The good news concerns the whole world that God made and that waits for its deliverance (Romans 8:19–21).
vv: [[Now after he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.

The NRSV prints the double brackets to show that this ending is missing from the oldest manuscripts. The first witness is a woman whom Jesus had delivered. The one who had been most bound is the first to see him risen from death.
But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it.
The Gospel is honest about the apostles. Their faith did not come easily, and that makes their witness more credible, not less.
Later he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were sitting at the table; and he upbraided them for their lack of faith and stubbornness,
Jesus rebukes them, and in the very next breath he sends them. He does not wait for perfect apostles. He makes apostles out of forgiven unbelievers.
And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.
The Church's mission in one sentence. The verb “go” turns the small upper room into a starting point for the whole world.
ch: The Council of Trent received the books of Scripture “with all their parts” as they are read in the Church, and this longer ending of Mark has always been read as Scripture. The Catechism cites the next verse, “The one who believes and is baptized will be saved” (16:16), to show that the Lord tied the forgiveness of sins to faith and baptism (CCC 977, 1257). It also notes the apostles' doubt, and draws the lesson that their faith in the Resurrection was born of the risen Lord's action, not of their own imagination (CCC 643–644).

qa: If the longer ending of Mark is not in the oldest manuscripts, is it really Scripture?

Yes. The Church received it in her canon, and the Council of Trent confirmed the books of Scripture with all their parts as they are read in the Church. Whether the evangelist himself wrote these verses is a question of history; that they are inspired and belong to the Gospel is a matter of the Church's faith. Many other parts of the Bible also took shape through more than one hand.
Did Peter and John disobey lawful authority?

They were respectful and asked the council itself to judge. But no human authority can order someone to deny what God has done. The Church teaches obedience to legitimate authority, and also that we must refuse a command that is against God's law (Acts 5:29; CCC 2242). Their way of refusing was peaceful: they kept speaking and they prayed.
rite: Saturday of the Easter Octave closes the white week of the newly baptized. In the ancient Roman practice they wore their white baptismal garments through the Octave and laid them aside at its end, which is why the next Sunday was known in Latin as Dominica in albis. Tonight's First Vespers already belongs to the Second Sunday of Easter, the Sunday of Divine Mercy. A good family custom for today: each person names one thing they have “seen and heard” of God this past week.
study: People recognised that Peter and John “had been with Jesus”. What would show others that I have been with him?
The council could not deny the sign, yet it avoided it. Is there a truth I know but keep avoiding?
The apostles believed slowly. How does their honesty help my own doubts?
Christ sent forgiven unbelievers into the world. To whom is he sending me this week?

lead: The eighth day after Easter brings us back to the upper room, “a week later”, and the Gospel is the same in all three years of the Lectionary: the risen Lord breathes the Holy Spirit on the apostles and gives them power to forgive sins, and then he meets Thomas. Everything else today gathers around that Gospel. Acts shows the community that the Resurrection has made: one heart and soul, nobody in need. Psalm 118, the great Easter psalm, sings that his steadfast love endures forever. The First Letter of John tells the believer that faith is the victory that conquers the world, and points to the one who came by water and blood.

Since the year 2000, by decision of St John Paul II, this Sunday is also called the Sunday of Divine Mercy. The readings fit the title well: mercy in the forgiveness of sins (John), mercy in the sharing of goods (Acts), mercy that endures forever (the psalm), mercy flowing as water and blood (1 John). The optional Sequence of Easter may still be sung today. The key words are peace, mercy and believe.

r.h: One heart and soul
set: This is the second of Luke's summaries of life in the first Jerusalem community (the first is 2:42–47; the third, 5:12–16). Each describes what the Church looked like when the Spirit had just been given. This one comes straight after the community has prayed for boldness and been shaken by the Spirit (4:23–31). Luke goes on at once to two contrasting examples: Barnabas, who gives generously (4:36–37), and Ananias and Sapphira, who pretend to (5:1–11).
str: v. 32: one heart and soul; no one claims anything as his own; all held in common.
v. 33: great power in the apostles' testimony to the Resurrection; great grace on all.
vv. 34–35: no one in need; owners sell and lay the price at the apostles' feet; each receives as he needs.
kw: A Greek proverb said that friends have one soul. Luke goes further: the whole community, not only a pair of friends, is one. The unity is the work of the Spirit, not of agreement alone.

The sharing was a willing act of love, not a law: Peter will say to Ananias that the land and the money remained his own to dispose of (5:4). What mattered was that nobody held on to his goods against a brother in need.
The word recalls Deuteronomy 15:4 in the Greek Old Testament: “there will be no one in need among you”. The promise of the law is fulfilled in the community of the Risen One.
vv: Now the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed private ownership of any possessions, but everything they owned was held in common.
Unity of heart comes first, then the sharing of goods. The second grows out of the first.
With great power the apostles gave their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.
This verse stands in the middle of a passage about money, and it explains it. A community that believes Christ is risen can hold its possessions loosely.
There was not a needy person among them,
This is the test Luke applies. The measure of a Christian community is not only how well it prays, but whether anyone among them is left in need.
They laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need.
To lay something at someone's feet was a sign of handing it over to his authority. The gifts are entrusted to the apostles, and from the start the Church's care for the poor is organised and ordered.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of the communion of saints, quotes this verse: everything the true Christian has is to be regarded as a good possessed in common with everyone else, and Christians should be ready to come to the help of the needy (CCC 952). The Church has never made common ownership a law for all; she defends the right to private property and also teaches the universal destination of goods (CCC 2402–2404). Religious communities, which hold their goods in common, have always looked to this passage, and St Augustine's Rule opens with it (in substance).

r.h: His steadfast love endures forever
set: Psalm 118 is the last of the Hallel psalms (113–118), sung at the great feasts of Israel and at the Passover meal. It was very likely the hymn Jesus and the disciples sang before going out to the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:26). It is a song of thanksgiving by someone rescued from death, entering the Temple gates in procession, and the whole people joins in. The Church sings it throughout the Easter Octave.
str: vv. 2–4: a three-part call: Israel, the house of Aaron, those who fear the Lord: his steadfast love endures forever.
vv. 13–15: “I was pushed hard, so that I was falling, but the Lord helped me”; songs of victory.
vv. 22–24: the rejected stone; this is the Lord's doing; this is the day the Lord has made.
kw: God's faithful covenant love, the love that does not give up. The Latin version renders it misericordia, mercy, and so this psalm stands well on the Sunday of Divine Mercy.
In the psalm, the one rejected and then rescued; in the New Testament, Christ rejected and raised (Matthew 21:42; Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7).
vv: Let Israel say, “His steadfast love endures forever.”
The refrain was a response sung by the people. The Church sings it with Israel, not instead of Israel.
I was pushed hard, so that I was falling, but the Lord helped me.
On Easter lips this is the voice of Christ, who was pushed all the way into death and was raised up.
This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.
The Roman liturgy sings this verse throughout the Easter Octave. Each day of the eight is counted as one great day.
ch: Jesus himself applies verse 22 to his rejection (Mark 12:10–11), and the apostles proclaim it of his Resurrection (Acts 4:11). The Church has made verse 24 the song of Easter, and in the Roman Rite it is sung in the Gradual or the responsory at Easter and through the Octave. On this Sunday the refrain “his steadfast love endures forever” becomes the Church's thanks for Divine Mercy.

r.h: This is the victory that conquers the world
set: The First Letter of John was written in the circle of the Fourth Gospel, toward the end of the first century, to communities troubled by people who had left them (2:19). Some of those who left seem to have denied that Jesus truly came in the flesh (4:2–3). The letter keeps returning to two tests of true faith: to believe rightly about Jesus, and to love one's brothers and sisters. In these verses the two tests come together. Throughout the Easter season, Year B reads from this letter on its Sundays.
str: v. 1: whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God; whoever loves the parent loves the child.
vv. 2–3: love of God shows itself in keeping his commandments, which are not burdensome.
vv. 4–5: what is born of God conquers the world; our faith is the victory.
v. 6: the one who came by water and blood; the Spirit testifies.
kw: A theme of John's Gospel and letters (John 1:13; 3:3–5). Faith is not only an opinion. It is a new birth, the life of a child of God.
The only time this noun occurs in the New Testament. It echoes Jesus' words at the Last Supper: “take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

Many scholars think John means Jesus' baptism in the Jordan and his death on the Cross: he did not only come by water, as some taught, but truly suffered and died. Many Fathers also heard an echo of the water and blood from his pierced side (John 19:34).
vv: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the parent loves the child.
A family logic: if you love the Father, you love his children. Love of God and love of neighbour are not two loves but one.
For the love of God is this, that we obey his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome,
Not because they are easy, but because the one who is born of God has received the strength to keep them. Love makes the yoke light (Matthew 11:30).
for whatever is born of God conquers the world. And this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith.
The “world” here means the power that opposes God. The victory has already been won by Christ, and faith is how we share in it.
This is the one who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ, not with the water only but with the water and the blood.
John insists on the blood: the Christ who saves us truly died. A Christianity without the Cross is not the faith of the apostles.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the blood and water that flowed from the pierced side of the crucified Jesus are types of Baptism and the Eucharist, the sacraments of new life (CCC 1225). Many Fathers saw the Church herself born from the side of Christ (CCC 766). The image of Divine Mercy given to St Faustina shows two rays, pale and red, streaming from the heart of Jesus; she understood them as the water and blood, which make souls righteous and give them life.

r.h: My Lord and my God!
set: It is the evening of the first Easter day. The disciples are behind locked doors “for fear of the Jews”. In John's Gospel this phrase usually means the Temple authorities who had handed Jesus over, not the Jewish people as such; the disciples themselves were Jews. Jesus comes through the locked doors, as the Risen One who is no longer bound by space.

The passage has two scenes a week apart, both on the first day of the week, and an ending (vv. 30–31) that tells us why the whole Gospel was written. Thomas, absent the first time, sets his own conditions for believing. The second Sunday answers him.
str: vv. 19–20: evening of the first day; locked doors; “Peace be with you”; hands and side; joy.
vv. 21–23: “As the Father has sent me, so I send you”; he breathes on them; the power to forgive and retain sins.
vv. 24–25: Thomas absent: “Unless I see … I will not believe.”
vv. 26–29: a week later; “Put your finger here”; “My Lord and my God!”; “Blessed are those who have not seen.”
vv. 30–31: why this book was written: that you may believe and have life.
kw: The ordinary Jewish greeting, shalom. On the lips of the risen Lord it becomes the gift he promised at the Supper (14:27), and it is said to men who had abandoned him. It is the first word of mercy.
The same rare verb the Greek Old Testament uses when God breathes the breath of life into the first man (Genesis 2:7). The risen Christ begins a new creation.
a week later (literally, after eight days)
Counted in the ancient way, this is again the first day of the week. From the start the risen Lord meets his Church on Sunday.
vv: When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors of the house where the disciples had met were locked for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”
Fear locks doors, and Jesus comes through them. He does not reproach the disciples for running away. His first word is peace.
When he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.”
The first gift of the Risen One to his Church is the power to forgive. Mercy is not left to feelings. It is entrusted to the apostles as a ministry.
Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.”
Jesus takes up Thomas's own conditions, almost word for word. He had heard. He meets the doubter where he is, and offers him the wounds.
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
The highest confession of faith in the Gospels. John's Gospel began, “the Word was God” (1:1), and it ends its main part on the lips of a doubter who now believes.
Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.
The last beatitude of the Gospels, and it is spoken for us. Every generation after the apostles believes through their word (17:20).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the risen Lord gave the apostles his own power to forgive sins when he breathed on them, and it cites this text as the institution of the sacrament of Penance (CCC 976, 1461, 1485). The Council of Trent taught the same. It takes Thomas's words as a confession of Jesus' divinity (CCC 448), and notes the apostles' doubt as evidence that their faith was not their own invention (CCC 644). St Gregory the Great preached that the unbelief of Thomas did more for our faith than the faith of the believing disciples, because as he touched the wounds he healed the wound of our doubt (in substance).

qa: Why is this called the Sunday of Divine Mercy?

St Faustina Kowalska, a Polish sister who died in 1938, recorded in her diary that Jesus asked for a feast of mercy on the Sunday after Easter. When St John Paul II canonized her on 30 April 2000, he declared that this Sunday would be called Divine Mercy Sunday throughout the Church, and the Congregation for Divine Worship decreed it that year. The name adds to the Sunday; it does not replace it. Its Mass and readings remain those of the Second Sunday of Easter, and they are already a feast of mercy.
Is “For fear of the Jews” anti-Jewish?

No. Jesus and all his disciples were Jews. In John's Gospel “the Jews” often means the Temple authorities who opposed Jesus, and the disciples feared that they would be arrested next. The Church teaches that the Jewish people as a whole are not to be blamed for Christ's death, and must never be presented as rejected or accursed (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
Does John 20:23 really mean confession to a priest?

The Church has always understood these words as giving the apostles and their successors the power to forgive and to retain sins (CCC 1461). To forgive or retain, they must know what the sins are, so the sacrament includes confession by the penitent, and the bishops and priests exercise this ministry (CCC 1456, 1461). The Council of Trent taught that this is the meaning of the text.
rite: In the Roman Rite this Sunday ends the Octave of Easter, and it was once called Dominica in albis, “Sunday in white”, when the newly baptized laid aside their white robes. Many parishes add devotions of Divine Mercy after Mass or at three in the afternoon: the image with the words “Jesus, I trust in you”, the Chaplet of Divine Mercy, and confession. A plenary indulgence was granted for this day in 2002 on the usual conditions (sacramental confession, Communion, prayer for the Pope's intentions, and detachment from all sin). The heart of the feast is in the Gospel itself: go to confession, and receive the mercy that Christ entrusted to his Church on the first Easter evening.
study: Jesus' first word to the disciples who had abandoned him was “Peace”. Whom do I need to greet with peace rather than reproach?
When did I last receive the sacrament of Penance? What keeps me from it?
“There was not a needy person among them.” What does that ask of my parish and my family?
Thomas believed when he saw the wounds. Where do I meet the wounds of Christ today, in the poor, the sick, the suffering?

lead: This year 25 March fell on Holy Thursday. When the Annunciation falls in Holy Week or the Easter Octave, the Roman calendar moves it to the Monday after the Second Sunday of Easter, and so the Church celebrates it today, in the white of Easter. It is a solemnity of the Lord: the day the Word became flesh in the womb of the Virgin Mary. The Gloria is sung, and in the Creed all kneel at the words “and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man”.

The readings are built on two answers of “Here I am”. Isaiah promises King Ahaz a sign he did not want: a young woman who will bear a son called Immanuel, God with us. Psalm 40 sings, “Here I am; in the scroll of the book it is written of me”, and the Letter to the Hebrews puts those words on the lips of the Son entering the world: “See, I have come to do your will.” In the Gospel Mary answers the angel: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord.” The Son's yes to the Father and Mary's yes to God meet in one moment. The key words are sign, body and yes.

r.h: God is with us
set: About the year 734 BC the kings of Aram (Damascus) and of the northern kingdom of Israel marched against Jerusalem to force Judah into their alliance against Assyria. King Ahaz of Judah, a descendant of David, was terrified: “his heart and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind” (7:2). Isaiah went to meet him with God's word: stand firm and do not fear. Ahaz had in fact already decided to buy the protection of the king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:7–8).
The Lectionary adds a single verse from the next chapter, 8:10, which ends with the meaning of the child's name: “for God is with us”.
str: vv. 10–11: God offers Ahaz a sign, as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven.
v. 12: Ahaz refuses, with pious words.
v. 13: Isaiah's rebuke to the house of David.
v. 14: the Lord himself will give a sign: a young woman, a son, Immanuel.
8:10: the plans of the nations will fail, for God is with us.
kw: In Isaiah a sign is a visible pledge that God will keep his word. Ahaz is offered any sign he likes, and refuses, because he does not want to depend on God.

The Hebrew word means a young woman of marriageable age; it does not in itself say “virgin”. The Greek Old Testament, made by Jewish translators about two centuries before Christ, rendered it parthenos, “virgin”, and Matthew quotes that form (Matthew 1:23). The Lectionary follows it, and the NRSV prints the Hebrew sense.
The name is a short confession of faith. In Isaiah it promises God's presence with the house of David in danger. In Christ, God is with us in person.
vv: Ask a sign of the Lord your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven.

God's offer is limitless: from the depths of the underworld to the heights of the sky. St Irenaeus saw in this range a hint of the Son who would come down from heaven and go down even to the dead (in substance).
But Ahaz said, I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test.
The words sound devout, and they quote the law (Deuteronomy 6:16). But Ahaz is not being humble. He has already put his trust in Assyria, and he does not want God to interfere.
Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Look, the young woman is with child and shall bear a son, and shall name him Immanuel.

Many scholars think that in Isaiah's own day the sign was the birth of a royal child, perhaps the future king Hezekiah, which showed that God had not abandoned David's line. The Church, following Matthew, sees the full meaning of the prophecy in the virgin birth of Jesus, the son of David who is truly God with us.
speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us.
The nations make plans, and God's presence brings them to nothing. The verse is the name Immanuel spelled out.
ch: St Matthew sees this prophecy fulfilled when Jesus is conceived of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:22–23). The Catechism teaches that the virginal conception is a divine work beyond human understanding and possibility, and cites Matthew's reading of Isaiah (CCC 497). The Second Vatican Council names this text among the Old Testament passages that, read in the light of the fuller revelation, bring the figure of the Mother of the Redeemer gradually into clearer light (Lumen Gentium 55). The king refused the sign; the Virgin, as the Gospel shows, received it.

r.h: Here I am; I come to do your will
set: Psalm 40 is the song of someone whom God has lifted out of “the desolate pit” (v. 2). Having been rescued, he asks what offering he should bring, and learns that God wants more than animals on the altar. He wants a person who listens and obeys. This teaching is found in the prophets too (1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6). Liturgical books count the psalm's title as verse 1, so verses 7–11 there are verses 6–10 in the NRSV.
str: v. 6: sacrifice and offering you do not desire, but you have given me an open ear.
vv. 7–8: “Here I am”; the scroll; your law is within my heart.
vv. 9–10: I have told the glad news in the great congregation; I have not hidden your saving help.
kw: you have given me an open ear

Literally “ears you have dug for me”: you have opened a channel for your word. The Greek Old Testament, followed by Hebrews 10:5, has “a body you have prepared for me”. The ear that hears and the body that offers itself are two sides of the same obedience.
The word of a servant presenting himself for duty. Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Isaiah answer God with the same readiness.
vv: Sacrifice and offering you do not desire, but you have given me an open ear.
The psalm does not condemn Israel's worship. It says what all worship is for: a listening heart.
Then I said, “Here I am; in the scroll of the book it is written of me.
The psalmist finds his life already written in God's word. The Church hears Christ say this of himself, for the whole of Scripture speaks of him (Luke 24:44).
I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart.”
The law written on the heart is the promise of the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33). Obedience here is not a burden but a delight.
ch: The Letter to the Hebrews reads these verses as the words of Christ at the moment of the Incarnation (Hebrews 10:5–7), and the Catechism takes them up in the same way (CCC 462). On this feast the psalm becomes the prayer that unites the Son's obedience and Mary's: the response “Here I am, Lord; I come to do your will” is sung by the whole Church.

r.h: A body you have prepared for me
set: The Letter to the Hebrews was written to Christians, very likely of Jewish background, who were tempted to look back to the Temple and its sacrifices. Its author is unknown; the early Church often linked it with St Paul, though its style is very different from his letters. Chapters 8 to 10 compare the yearly sacrifices of the Day of Atonement with the one offering of Christ. Here the author quotes Psalm 40 in its Greek form and hears it as Christ's own prayer on coming into the world.
str: v. 4: the blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins.
vv. 5–7: Christ's words on coming into the world: a body you have prepared for me; I have come to do your will.
vv. 8–9: the first is taken away so that the second may stand.
v. 10: by that will we are sanctified through the offering of Jesus' body once for all.
kw: The Greek of Psalm 40 has “a body” where the Hebrew has “ears”. The author sees in it the Incarnation: the Son takes a body in order to offer it.
The word appears three times in these verses. The heart of Christ's sacrifice is not the suffering in itself but loving obedience to the Father's will.
Christ's offering is unique and complete. It does not need to be repeated, and nothing can be added to it.
vv: For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.
The sacrifices of the law were given by God and were truly holy. But they pointed beyond themselves to the offering that would do what they could only promise.
Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body you have prepared for me;
The Annunciation is the moment of these words. In Mary's womb the Son receives the body he will offer on the Cross.
then he added, “See, I have come to do your will.” He abolishes the first in order to establish the second.
“The first” is the order of animal sacrifices; “the second” is the doing of God's will by the Son. Israel's worship is not despised. It reaches its goal.
And it is by God’s will that we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
The body that began in Nazareth is the body offered on Calvary and given in the Eucharist. From the first moment to the last, Christ's life is one offering.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it teaches why the Word became flesh (CCC 462), and when it speaks of Christ's whole life as an offering to the Father, from his entry into the world to the Cross (CCC 606, 614). The Mass is not another sacrifice added to this one. It makes present the one sacrifice of the Cross, offered once for all (CCC 1366–1367). On this feast the Church sees the beginning and the end of Christ's offering together: “See, I have come” in Nazareth, and “It is finished” on Golgotha.

r.h: Here am I, the servant of the Lord
set: Luke tells two annunciations side by side. Six months earlier the angel Gabriel appeared to Zechariah, a priest, in the Temple of Jerusalem, at the hour of incense (1:5–25). Now he is sent to a young woman in Nazareth, an unknown village in Galilee. Zechariah doubted and was struck silent; Mary asks a question and believes. The parallel is deliberate.

Mary is betrothed to Joseph. In Jewish custom of the time betrothal was a binding agreement, already a kind of marriage, though the bride did not yet live in her husband's house. Joseph is “of the house of David”, and so the child will legally belong to David's line.
str: vv. 26–27: the sixth month; Gabriel; Nazareth; a virgin betrothed to Joseph; her name was Mary.
vv. 28–29: “Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you”; she is perplexed.
vv. 30–33: do not be afraid; you will conceive and bear a son, Jesus; the throne of David; a kingdom without end.
vv. 34–35: “How can this be?”; the Holy Spirit, the power of the Most High; Son of God.
vv. 36–37: Elizabeth; nothing is impossible with God.
v. 38: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
kw: A perfect passive participle of the verb “to grace”: one who has been graced and remains so. It stands in place of her name. The Church sees in it the fullness of grace given to Mary from the first moment of her existence (CCC 490–491).

The same verb the Greek Old Testament uses for the cloud of God's glory that settled on the tent of meeting (Exodus 40:35), and Luke uses it again of the cloud at the Transfiguration (9:34). Mary becomes the dwelling of God's presence.
The feminine of the word for slave or servant. Mary takes the title of Israel's great servants of God. Her true liberty is to belong wholly to God.
vv: And he came to her and said, “Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you.”

The Greek greeting chaire means literally “rejoice”. Many scholars hear in it the prophets' call to Daughter Zion: “Rejoice … the Lord is in your midst” (Zephaniah 3:14–17). The Lord who was promised to dwell in Zion is about to dwell in her.
He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give to him the throne of his ancestor David.
The words take up God's promise to David through the prophet Nathan (2 Samuel 7:12–16). What Ahaz would not believe is now fulfilled: the house of David has its everlasting king.
Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, since I am a virgin?”

Mary does not doubt the promise. She asks how it will happen. Many Fathers, among them St Augustine, read in her question an intention to remain a virgin (in substance). The angel's answer shows that this child will come from God alone.
The angel said to her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be holy; he will be called Son of God.
The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation now comes upon Mary for the new creation. The conception of Jesus is the work of the Holy Spirit, not of any man.
Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.” Then the angel departed from her.
Her yes is given in faith, without knowing what it will cost. The Greek verb genoito expresses a wish: not resignation, but glad desire.
ch: The Catechism teaches that at the Annunciation Mary gave the consent of faith, and that by this yes she became the Mother of God and gave herself entirely to the person and work of her Son (CCC 494–495). It quotes St Irenaeus: the knot of Eve's disobedience was untied by Mary's obedience (CCC 494; Lumen Gentium 56). It also teaches the virginal conception as the work of the Spirit (CCC 484–486, 497), and sees in Mary's “let it be with me” at the Annunciation the heart of Christian prayer (CCC 2617). St Bernard, in a homily on this Gospel, pictures the whole world waiting on Mary's answer and begging her to reply (in substance). The Church repeats this mystery three times a day in the Angelus, which in Eastertide gives way to the Regina caeli.

qa: Why does the NRSV say “young woman” in Isaiah 7:14 when the Lectionary says “virgin”?

The Hebrew word ‘almâ means a young woman of marriageable age. The Greek translation made by Jews before Christ rendered it “virgin” (parthenos), and Matthew quotes it in that form. The NRSV translates the Hebrew; the Lectionary follows the Greek and Matthew. The Church's faith in the virginal conception rests on the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, which say plainly that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit without a human father (CCC 496–497). Isaiah's sign finds its fullest meaning there.
Why is the Annunciation a feast of the Lord rather than of Mary?

Because it celebrates the Incarnation: the Word made flesh. Mary is at the centre of the Gospel scene, and her yes is honoured, but the solemnity is the beginning of our salvation in Christ. Since the reform of the calendar in 1969 it has been called the Annunciation of the Lord. Christmas, nine months later, completes it.
Does “full of grace” mean Mary did not need a Saviour?

No. Mary was redeemed by Christ, in a more exalted way: she was preserved from all stain of original sin from the first moment of her conception, by the merits of her Son (Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus, 1854; CCC 491–492). Mary herself calls God “my Saviour” (Luke 1:47).
rite: Because this solemnity falls in Eastertide this year, the double Alleluia continues at the dismissal and the paschal candle stands lit beside the altar or ambo. Today, at the words of the Creed “and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man”, the people kneel, as they do on Christmas Day. In the Roman tradition this feast also turns our thoughts to the dignity of human life from its beginning, for the Son of God was himself an unborn child. Families might pray the Regina caeli together today and remember that the Easter joy began in a quiet house in Nazareth.
study: Ahaz refused a sign because he had already made his own plans. Where do I avoid asking God, so that he will not interfere?
Mary asked, “How can this be?” and then said yes. How do I bring my honest questions to God without closing my heart?
Christ's first words on entering the world were “I have come to do your will”. What would change if I began each day with those words?
The Word became flesh in an unborn child. How does this feast shape the way I treat the unborn, the poor and the forgotten?

lead: The first reading repeats Sunday's picture of the Jerusalem community, one heart and soul, and adds a name: Joseph, called Barnabas, the son of encouragement, who sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet. The Gospel continues the night conversation with Nicodemus. Being born from above is the work of the Spirit, who blows like the wind, and the Son of Man must be lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness. Psalm 93 sings that the Lord is king. The key words today are encouragement, Spirit and lifted up.

r.h: Barnabas, son of encouragement
set: Luke follows his summary of the community's sharing (vv. 32–35, read on Sunday) with a concrete example. Barnabas will become one of the great figures of Acts: he vouches for Saul when the disciples fear him (9:27), is sent to the new Church at Antioch (11:22–24), and travels with Paul on the first mission (13:2).
str: vv. 32–35: one heart and soul; great power in the witness to the Resurrection; no one in need.
vv. 36–37: Joseph Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus, sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet.
kw: Paraklēsis means encouragement, comfort, exhortation. It is related to Paraklētos, the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit (John 14:16). Barnabas's new name describes his gift: he lifts others up.
A member of the tribe of Levi, which served in the Temple. The law gave the Levites no tribal land (Numbers 18:20), though by this time some, like Barnabas, owned property.
vv: Now the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul,
Unity of heart comes before any sharing of goods, and makes it possible.
There was a Levite, a native of Cyprus, Joseph, to whom the apostles gave the name Barnabas (which means “son of encouragement”).
A new name marks a new life, as with Simon who became Peter. The apostles name him for what grace has made of him.
He sold a field that belonged to him, then brought the money, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
Luke names him because the gift was real and whole. The next chapter shows the opposite in Ananias and Sapphira (5:1–11).
ch: The Catechism, on the communion of saints, quotes the words about holding everything in common, and urges Christians to be ready to help the needy (CCC 952). The Church keeps the memorial of St Barnabas, apostle, on 11 June. A parish needs people with his gift: those who welcome newcomers, vouch for the doubtful, and give without being asked.

r.h: So must the Son of Man be lifted up
set: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader of his people, has come to Jesus by night (3:1–2). Jesus has told him that no one can see the kingdom of God without being born anōthen, a word that means both “again” and “from above”. Nicodemus took the first meaning; Jesus means the second. Nicodemus appears again later, defending Jesus (7:50–51) and bringing spices for his burial (19:39).
str: vv. 7b–8: you must be born from above; the wind blows where it chooses.
vv. 9–12: “How can these things be?”; earthly and heavenly things.
v. 13: no one has ascended except the one who descended.
vv. 14–15: as Moses lifted up the serpent, so the Son of Man; eternal life for whoever believes.
kw: One Greek word for both, as Hebrew rûaḥ. Jesus plays on it: you cannot see the wind, only its effects. So it is with those born of the Spirit.
In John this verb means both the lifting up on the Cross and the exaltation to glory (8:28; 12:32–33). The Cross is already the throne.
vv: The wind blows where it chooses, and you hear the sound of it, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes.
New birth is not something we produce. It is received, like the wind, from God.
No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.
Only the one who came from the Father can speak of heavenly things. In him heaven and earth are joined.
And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,

In Numbers 21:8–9 those bitten by serpents looked at the bronze serpent and lived. The Book of Wisdom says they were saved not by what they saw but by God, the Saviour of all (Wisdom 16:7). So we look to the crucified and live.
ch: The Catechism cites verse 13 when it teaches that Christ's Ascension is bound up with his first descent from heaven in the Incarnation (CCC 661), and it reads the new birth of water and Spirit as baptism (CCC 1215). St Augustine, preaching on this Gospel, says that as the Israelites looked on the serpent and were healed of its bite, so we look on Christ crucified and are healed of sin (in substance).

qa: Was the bronze serpent an idol?

No. God commanded it, and it was a sign pointing to his healing power (Wisdom 16:6–7). Later, when people began to burn incense to it, King Hezekiah destroyed it (2 Kings 18:4). The Catechism mentions it as an example of an image that God himself ordained, pointing ahead to salvation through the Word made flesh (CCC 2130).
study: Barnabas was named for the way he encouraged others. Whom can I encourage this week?
Jesus says the Spirit blows where it chooses. Where have I seen the Spirit at work in a way I did not expect?

lead: On the memorial of St John Baptist de la Salle, patron of teachers, both readings speak of a light that cannot be locked away. In Acts the high priest’s party arrests the apostles a second time, and in the night an angel opens the prison and sends them back to teach in the temple. In John, the best-loved verse of the Gospel says where that light comes from: God so loved the world that he gave his only Son. Psalm 34 is the song of people who were rescued: “The Lord hears the cry of the poor”.

r.h: The prison that could not hold the word
set: Luke tells of two arrests of the apostles. In chapter 4 Peter and John were held overnight and warned not to speak in the name of Jesus. They went on speaking, signs multiplied, and crowds gathered in Solomon’s Portico (5:12–16). Now the high priest and his party arrest the apostles as a group.

The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who ran the temple. Acts 23:8 notes that they said there is no resurrection, no angel and no spirit. Luke lets the irony speak for itself: an angel releases men who preach the Resurrection.
str: vv. 17–18: jealousy and arrest.
vv. 19–21a: the angel opens the doors; at daybreak the apostles are teaching in the temple.
vv. 21b–24: the council gathers; the prison is found locked and empty.
vv. 25–26: the apostles are found teaching and brought back, without violence.
kw: The word can mean zeal or jealousy. Here it is the resentment of those whose authority feels threatened. Luke uses it again when the leaders in Pisidian Antioch see the crowds around Paul (13:45).
The priest who commanded the temple police, a guard of Levites. In the running of the temple he stood close in rank to the high priest.

Literally “the words of this life”. The angel does not say “this teaching” but “this life”. The Gospel is the life of the risen Christ offered to people; Peter has already called him “the Author of life” (3:15).
vv: But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out,

Acts tells of three such releases: here, Peter in 12:6–11, and Paul and Silas in 16:25–26. God does not always rescue his witnesses this way: Stephen and James will die (7:60; 12:2). But he shows that no human power can lock up his word.
Go, stand in the temple and tell the people the whole message about this life.
The angel does not send them into hiding but back to the most public place in Jerusalem. The release is given for witness, not for safety.
but without violence, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people.
The people held the apostles in high regard (5:13). Luke takes care to show that the opposition came from a group of leaders, not from the people of Jerusalem as a whole.
ch: Paul, writing from his own chains, puts the lesson of this scene in one line: “the word of God is not chained” (2 Timothy 2:9). The Church has read such stories with sober hope. Her witnesses are not always freed from prison, and many have died there, yet the word they carried has gone on. The courage of the apostles is not a gift of temperament. Luke shows it as the work of the Holy Spirit, whom they received at Pentecost.

r.h: God so loved the world
set: These verses close the night conversation with Nicodemus, the Pharisee who came to Jesus by night (3:1–2). Jesus has just said that the Son of Man must be lifted up as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness (3:14–15).

Ancient Greek had no quotation marks, and scholars differ on whether vv. 16–21 are still the words of Jesus or the evangelist’s own reflection on them. The NRSV keeps them within the words of Jesus. Either way the Church receives them as the word of God.
str: v. 16: the gift: God’s love gives the only Son.
vv. 17–18: the purpose: to save, not to condemn.
vv. 19–21: the judgment: the light has come, and people show what they love by whether they come to it.
kw: Used of an only child, as of the widow’s son at Nain (Luke 7:12). In John it marks the unique Son, who is not one son among many. The Creed says “the Only Begotten Son of God”.
In John the world can be the creation God loves (3:16), and also humanity closed against God (15:18). God loves even the world that does not love him back.
Both a verdict and the separation it brings about. Jesus does not come to pass sentence; his coming is itself the light in which people decide.
vv: For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son,

“Gave” looks toward the cross, since Jesus has just spoken of being lifted up (3:14). Paul says the same in other words: “He who did not withhold his own Son, but gave him up for all of us” (Romans 8:32).
God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world,
The Catechism teaches that the Son did not come to judge but to save, and that whoever rejects grace in this life already judges himself (CCC 679).
But those who do what is true come to the light,
Not “those who know the truth” but those who do it. In John truth is something lived. Nicodemus, who came by night, will come into the open at the burial of Jesus (19:39).
ch: The Catechism places John 3:16 among the texts that say why the Word became flesh: so that we might know the love of God (CCC 458). Verse 18 speaks of refusing the light, not of never having seen it. The Church teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel but seek God with a sincere heart can also attain salvation by his grace (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847).

qa: Does John 3:16 mean that only believing matters, and not how we live?

No. The same passage ends with deeds: those who do evil hate the light, and those who do what is true come to it (3:20–21). Faith in John means coming into the light and living in it. The Catechism teaches that faith deprived of hope and love does not fully unite the believer to Christ, and quotes James: faith apart from works is dead (CCC 1815).
rite: St John Baptist de la Salle (1651–1719) was a priest and canon of Reims who gave up his canonry and his family wealth to found the Brothers of the Christian Schools, religious brothers who are teachers and not priests. He opened schools for poor boys, taught reading in French before Latin, and trained teachers with great care. He died on Good Friday, 7 April 1719, near Rouen, and Pope Pius XII named him patron of teachers in 1950. Like the apostles sent back to “tell the people”, those who teach the young share in the Church’s work of light.
study: Where does my faith stay locked away, and where is the Lord sending me back to speak, gently and in the open?
John 3:16 is often quoted. What changes if I read it slowly, with my own name in place of “the world”?

lead: The apostles brought back from the temple now stand before the council, and Peter gives the answer that has steadied Christians ever since: “We must obey God rather than any human authority.” He calls himself a witness, together with the Holy Spirit. The Gospel speaks of another witness, the one who comes from above and testifies to what he has seen and heard. Psalm 34 again promises that the Lord is near to the brokenhearted.

r.h: Obey God rather than any human authority
set: This follows straight on from yesterday’s reading in Acts 5:17–26. The council, the Sanhedrin, was the highest Jewish court in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest; at this time that was probably Caiaphas, who held office until about AD 36. Earlier the apostles had been ordered not to speak in the name of Jesus (4:18). They have been found teaching in the temple.
str: vv. 27–28: the high priest’s charge: disobedience, and an accusation of blame.
vv. 29–32: Peter’s answer: obedience to God, the Resurrection, and witness.
v. 33: the council’s fury.
kw: Literally “to obey one in authority”. It frames Peter’s answer: we must obey God (v. 29), and God gives the Spirit to those who obey him (v. 32). Obedience to God is the source of their freedom before men.

A rich word: leader, founder, pioneer, the one who goes first and opens the way. Peter called Jesus “the Author of life” with the same word (3:15), and Hebrews calls him “the pioneer” of our salvation and of our faith (2:10; 12:2).
A witness tells what he has seen. In the Church the word came to mean those who bear witness to the point of death, the martyrs. Here the human witness and the Spirit’s witness go together.
vv: you are determined to bring this man’s blood on us.

The leaders fear being held responsible for the death of Jesus. Peter does not answer with revenge. He offers repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel (v. 31). The Church teaches that the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
We must obey God rather than any human authority.

Educated readers of Greek would have thought of Socrates, who told his judges in Athens that he would obey the god rather than them (Plato, Apology 29d). The Catechism cites this verse: a citizen is bound in conscience not to follow the directives of civil authorities when they are contrary to the moral order and to the Gospel (CCC 2242).
whom you had killed by hanging him on a tree.

“Tree” recalls Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where one hanged on a tree is under a curse. Paul says that Christ became a curse for us to redeem us (Galatians 3:13). What looked like God’s rejection was the way of our redemption.
And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit
At the Last Supper Jesus promised this double witness: the Spirit “will testify on my behalf. You also are to testify” (John 15:26–27).
ch: The Church has always read verse 29 as the charter of conscience. It does not make Christians disobedient citizens: Peter and Paul teach respect for rulers (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). But when a human command contradicts God’s law, obedience to God comes first. The martyrs of every age, from Stephen onward, have lived this verse.

r.h: The one who comes from above
set: Just before this passage John the Baptist gives his last witness to Jesus: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (3:30). It is not clear whether vv. 31–36 continue the Baptist’s words or are the evangelist’s comment. Many commentators read them as the evangelist’s reflection, gathering up the themes of the whole chapter: from above, testimony, Spirit, life.
str: vv. 31–32: the one from above and the one from the earth.
vv. 33–34: accepting his testimony; the words of God and the Spirit.
vv. 35–36: the Father’s love for the Son and the choice it sets before us.
kw: The same word as in 3:3, where it can mean both “again” and “from above”. Jesus is from above by origin; believers are born from above by grace.
To set one’s seal on a document is to confirm it as true. Whoever accepts Christ’s testimony puts his own seal on the truth of God.
Not a passing temper in God, but his holiness turned against sin. The Greek says it “remains” (menei) on the one who refuses the Son: it is what is left when life is refused.
vv: The one who comes from above is above all;
John the Baptist was the greatest of the prophets, yet he speaks as one “of the earth”. Jesus alone speaks from heaven, because he comes from there.
for he gives the Spirit without measure.

The Greek does not say who gives. It may mean that God gives the Spirit to the Son without measure, or that the Son gives the Spirit without measure to believers. Both are true: the Son receives all from the Father and pours it out (John 1:16).
The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands.
John repeats this at the Last Supper: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands” (13:3) rose and washed the disciples’ feet. Everything placed in his hands is used to serve.
ch: The Church reads these verses as a summary of faith in the Son: he comes from the Father, speaks the Father’s words, and gives the Spirit. Verse 36 places eternal life in the present tense: the believer “has” it already, as a gift begun in Baptism. The Church also teaches that this gift can be lost by grave sin and found again by repentance; final salvation remains a hope we pray for (CCC 1861; CCC 1821).

study: When has obeying God cost me something before other people? What helped me stand?
The Father has put all things into the hands of Jesus. What do I need to place there today?

lead: A wise teacher of the law gives the council a sober piece of advice: if this movement is of God, you cannot overthrow it. The apostles are flogged and leave rejoicing. In the Gospel, Jesus feeds five thousand people from five barley loaves, and the crowd wants to make him king; he withdraws to the mountain alone. With this sign John’s great chapter on the Bread of Life begins, read at Mass over the coming days. Psalm 27 gives the prayer of one who wants only to dwell in the house of the Lord.

r.h: If it is of God
set: Gamaliel, a Pharisee, was one of the most honoured teachers of the law of his time; Jewish tradition remembers him as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder. Paul later says that he was brought up “at the feet of Gamaliel” (22:3). The Pharisees, unlike the Sadducees, believed in the resurrection, and Gamaliel urges caution.

Gamaliel gives two examples of movements that came to nothing. Judas the Galilean led a revolt at the time of the Roman census in AD 6. The Jewish historian Josephus tells of a Theudas who rose up under the governor Fadus, around AD 45, which would be after this speech. Some think Gamaliel means an earlier man of the same name, a common one; others think Luke’s order here is loose. The point of the speech does not depend on it.
str: vv. 34–35: Gamaliel has the apostles put outside and speaks.
vv. 36–37: two movements that failed.
vv. 38–39: his counsel: let them alone.
v. 40: flogging and a fresh order of silence.
vv. 41–42: the apostles rejoice and keep preaching.
kw: A recognized master of the Law of Moses. Luke uses the word for the teachers of the law who sat listening to Jesus when he healed the paralysed man (Luke 5:17). Gamaliel is “respected by all the people”.
One Greek word: “God-fighters”. Gamaliel warns that resistance to a work of God is a fight that cannot be won.
for the sake of the name
“The name” stands for Jesus himself. In Acts the apostles heal, preach and suffer “in the name” (3:6; 4:12). To suffer for the name is to share his lot.
vv: if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them

A principle of discernment the Church has often recalled: time and fruit reveal what is of God. It is not the whole answer, since evil can last a long while, but it guards against hasty violence against what one does not understand.
they had them flogged.
Probably the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes, based on Deuteronomy 25:3. Paul says he received it five times (2 Corinthians 11:24).
they rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name.
Jesus had said, “Blessed are you when people hate you... on account of the Son of Man. Rejoice in that day” (Luke 6:22–23). The apostles find the beatitude true in their own bodies.
they did not cease to teach and proclaim Jesus as the Messiah.
“In the temple and at home”: the two places of the first Church, public worship and the house church. Luke ends this section with the word still going on.
ch: The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). Today’s apostles are not yet martyrs, but their joy in dishonour is the same spirit. Christians who are mocked or excluded for their faith in many lands today can read verse 41 as their own story, and pray, as the apostles did, for those who wrong them.

r.h: Five barley loaves for five thousand
set: The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle of Jesus’ ministry told in all four Gospels. John alone notes that it was near Passover, names Philip and Andrew, and mentions the boy and the barley loaves. Barley bread was the bread of the poor.
In John the miracle is a “sign”: it points beyond itself. It opens chapter 6, where Jesus will say, “I am the bread of life” (6:35), and speak of eating his flesh and drinking his blood (6:51–58).
str: vv. 1–4: Galilee, the mountain, the crowd, Passover near.
vv. 5–9: Jesus tests Philip; Andrew brings the boy’s loaves.
vv. 10–13: the people sit, eat their fill, and twelve baskets of fragments remain.
vv. 14–15: the crowd’s acclaim; Jesus withdraws to the mountain alone.
kw: From the verb that gives us the word Eucharist. John uses it here and again when he recalls this meal (6:23). Early readers could not miss the echo of the Lord’s Supper.

The broken pieces. The Didache, an early Christian writing, uses the same word for the eucharistic bread and prays that, as the broken bread once scattered on the hills was gathered into one, the Church may be gathered into God’s kingdom (in substance).
John’s word for the miracles of Jesus. A sign is meant to be read: the crowd sees the bread but must learn to see the giver.
vv: There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish.

An echo of Elisha, who fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, and “they ate, and had some left” (2 Kings 4:42–44). One greater than Elisha is here. The boy’s small gift, given up, becomes enough for all.
Then Jesus took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them
In the other Gospels the disciples hand out the bread. In John Jesus himself gives it, as he will give himself.
Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.
The Greek verb “be lost” returns in 6:39: the Father’s will is that Jesus “should lose nothing of all that he has given me”. The care for fragments is a picture of his care for every person.
to make him king, he withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
