The crowd wants a king who fills stomachs. Jesus will be proclaimed king only on the cross (19:19). He refuses a kingship that is not the Father’s way.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord says the blessing, breaks and distributes the loaves through his disciples to feed the multitude, prefigures the superabundance of the unique bread of his Eucharist (CCC 1335). The Church has also always read here a call to share bread with the hungry, since the Lord who feeds us with himself sends us to feed others.

qa: Was the miracle really just people sharing their food?

That reading is sometimes heard, but it is not what the text says. All four Gospels present a sign of Jesus’ power, and the crowd’s response, “This is indeed the prophet”, would make no sense if they had simply shared their lunches. Sharing is a true lesson drawn from the scene, but the Church believes in the miracle itself, as a sign of the Bread he gives.
study: What is my “five barley loaves”, the small thing I hesitate to hand over to Jesus?
How do I tell whether something new in my parish or my life is “of God”?

lead: The first Church meets its first quarrel, over food for widows, and solves it by sharing out ministry: the apostles keep to prayer and the word, and seven men full of the Spirit take up the daily service. In the Gospel the disciples cross the lake in the dark and the wind, and Jesus comes to them over the water: “It is I; do not be afraid.” Both scenes show a Church that is never left alone in its difficulties. Psalm 33 asks: “Lord, let your mercy be on us, as we place our trust in you”.

r.h: Seven men full of the Spirit
set: The Jerusalem Church was growing, and with growth came strain. “Hellenists” were Jewish believers who spoke Greek, many of them from Jewish communities outside the land who had settled in Jerusalem. “Hebrews” were Jewish believers whose everyday language was Aramaic. Both groups were Jewish; the difference was language and culture.

Widows without family had no income, and the Jerusalem community cared for them daily. The seven chosen all have Greek names, and one, Nicolaus, was a proselyte, a gentile who had become a Jew. The solution comes from within the group that felt neglected.
str: v. 1: the complaint.
vv. 2–4: the Twelve propose a solution.
vv. 5–6: the community chooses seven; the apostles pray and lay hands on them.
v. 7: the word spreads, even among the priests.
kw: The key word, used three ways: the daily “distribution” is diakonia (v. 1), “to wait on tables” is diakonein (v. 2), and the apostles’ “serving the word” is diakonia of the word (v. 4). Both are service; neither is lower in God’s eyes.
The word recalls Israel murmuring in the wilderness (Exodus 16). Luke does not hide the Church’s tensions, but shows how the Spirit heals them.
An ancient gesture of blessing and of handing on a task, used for Joshua by Moses (Numbers 27:18–23). In Acts it accompanies prayer and the gift of the Spirit.
vv: It is not right that we should neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables.
Not contempt for practical service, which the seven are chosen to do with the Spirit’s help. It is a question of each one’s calling: the apostles must not be pulled away from the word and prayer.
select from among yourselves seven men of good standing, full of the Spirit and of wisdom,
Even managing food requires the Spirit. The qualities asked for are spiritual before they are practical.
who prayed and laid their hands on them.
The community chooses, but the apostles commission them with prayer and the laying on of hands. The Church has seen in this the pattern of ordination.
a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
A striking note: many of the temple priests came to faith. The first Church was a Jewish community, and the Gospel took root first among the people of the covenant.
ch: Acts does not call the seven “deacons”, and two of them, Stephen and Philip, are soon seen preaching and baptizing. Yet since St Irenaeus in the second century the Church has seen in this scene the beginning of the diaconate. The Second Vatican Council teaches that deacons receive the laying on of hands “not unto the priesthood, but unto a ministry of service” (Lumen Gentium 29; CCC 1569).

r.h: It is I; do not be afraid
set: After the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus has withdrawn to the mountain to avoid being made king (6:15). The disciples set out alone across the lake toward Capernaum. Mark 6:45–52 and Matthew 14:22–33 tell the same event; Matthew adds Peter’s walk on the water. John’s account is short and leads straight to the next day’s discourse.
str: vv. 16–18: evening, darkness, a rough sea, and Jesus absent.
vv. 19–20: Jesus comes over the water and speaks.
v. 21: they want to take him in, and at once they reach land.
kw: In John darkness is never only the time of day. “It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them” describes the disciples’ state as much as the hour (cf. 1:5).
The Greek says “twenty-five or thirty stades”, about five or six kilometres. The NRSV gives “three or four miles”. They are in the middle of the lake, far from either shore.
Literally “I am”. On the lips of Jesus in John these words often recall the divine name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14), as in 8:58. Here they both identify him and reveal him.
vv: It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.
Many Christians know such nights: rowing hard with the Lord seemingly absent. John’s “not yet” promises that he is coming.
they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were terrified.
In the Old Testament it is God who “trampled the waves of the Sea” (Job 9:8). Jesus does what only God does.
It is I; do not be afraid.
The Lord’s first word is his presence, the second is peace. These are the words most often repeated in Scripture to frightened people.
immediately the boat reached the land toward which they were going.
Psalm 107 sings of sailors in a storm whom God brought “to their desired haven” (107:30). When Jesus is received, the journey reaches its end.
ch: From early times Christians have seen the boat as an image of the Church. Tertullian, writing on Baptism, says that the disciples’ little boat, tossed by the waves while the Lord slept, was a figure of the Church (in substance). The Church does not promise calm seas, but the presence of the Lord who comes over the waters and says, “It is I”.

study: Where in my parish or family is someone being overlooked, as the widows were? What could I do?
When has the Lord seemed absent while I was rowing in the dark? What helped me hear, “It is I”?

lead: On the Third Sunday of Easter all three readings speak of witness and forgiveness. In Acts Peter tells the crowd in the temple that they killed the Author of life, whom God raised, and at once offers them repentance and the wiping out of sins. In 1 John the Risen One is our advocate with the Father and the atoning sacrifice for the sins of the whole world. In Luke Jesus stands among the disciples, shows his hands and feet, eats before them, opens their minds to the Scriptures and sends them out: “You are witnesses of these things.” Psalm 4 prays, “Lord, let your face shine on us”. The thread is this: the Risen Lord is real, he forgives, and he makes witnesses.

r.h: The Author of life, whom God raised
set: Peter and John have healed a man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate of the temple (3:1–10). The crowd runs together in Solomon’s Portico, a colonnade along the eastern side of the temple court, and Peter explains what they have seen. This is his second great speech in Acts, after Pentecost.

The Lectionary leaves out verse 16, where Peter says that faith in the name of Jesus healed the man. The verses chosen keep the heart of the speech: what was done to Jesus, what God did, and what the hearers can do now.
str: vv. 13–15: a contrast: you handed him over and rejected him; God glorified and raised him.
vv. 17–18: you acted in ignorance; God fulfilled what the prophets foretold.
v. 19: the call: repent and turn, so that your sins may be wiped out.
kw: The Greek can mean servant or child. “God has glorified his servant” echoes the Greek of Isaiah 52:13, where, in the Greek, the Lord’s servant will be lifted up and glorified. Peter reads the suffering and glory of Jesus through the Servant Songs.
Leader, founder, the one who opens the way to life. Peter sets a sharp paradox: they asked for a murderer, a taker of life, and killed the giver of life.
Not innocence, but not full knowledge either. It echoes Jesus’ prayer on the cross: “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).
vv: has glorified his servant Jesus,
Peter begins with “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”. He speaks as a Jew to fellow Jews, of the God of their fathers, who has kept his promise in Jesus.
you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses.
The sentence turns on its middle: you killed, God raised. Human sin does not have the last word. “Witnesses” is the apostles’ title throughout Acts (1:8).
I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers.
Peter, who had himself denied Jesus, speaks with mercy. He calls them “friends” (literally “brothers”) and opens a door rather than closing one.
Repent therefore, and turn to God so that your sins may be wiped out,
“Wiped out” is the image of erasing writing from a tablet. The debt is not just covered; it is taken away.
ch: The Church teaches that the Passion of Christ cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism adds that sinners were the authors of Christ’s Passion, and that Christians, who know him and still sin, bear the graver responsibility (CCC 598). Peter’s “you” is therefore also our “we”. And his speech shows the right response: not blame, but repentance and the joy of forgiveness.

r.h: An advocate with the Father
set: The First Letter of John reads more like a homily than a letter. Tradition links it with the apostle John, and it shares the language of the Fourth Gospel; many scholars place it among the communities that treasured John’s Gospel, toward the end of the first century. A group had left the community (2:19), and some apparently claimed to be without sin (1:8–10).
John steers between two errors: saying that sin does not matter, and despairing because of sin. The answer to both is Christ.
str: v. 1a: the purpose: so that you may not sin.
vv. 1b–2: if anyone sins, Christ is our advocate and atoning sacrifice.
vv. 3–5a: the test of knowing God: keeping his commandments, his word.
kw: A tender word, used often in this letter. John writes as an old pastor to people he loves.
One called to stand beside another, especially in court. In the Gospel Jesus calls the Holy Spirit “another Advocate” (John 14:16); here Jesus himself is the Advocate before the Father.

The means by which sin is taken away and fellowship with God restored. In 4:10 John says that God himself sent his Son for this. It is not man appeasing an angry God, but God’s love providing the remedy.
vv: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin.
The goal is holiness, not mere forgiveness. Yet the next words admit at once that Christians do sin.
we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous;
St Augustine notes that John does not say “you have” but “we have”: the apostle counts himself among sinners who need an advocate (in substance, Homilies on the First Letter of John).
and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.
No one is outside the reach of the cross. The Catechism, citing this verse, teaches that Christ died for all without exception (CCC 605).
but whoever obeys his word, truly in this person the love of God has reached perfection.
“Love of God” can mean our love for God or God’s love in us; both come to completion in obedience. Knowledge of God is proved by a life, not only by words.
ch: The Catechism explains that Jesus himself is the first Paraclete, and that he promised the Spirit as “another” Paraclete (CCC 692). The Church receives the forgiveness promised here above all in Baptism and in the sacrament of Penance; John has just written that if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us (1:9; CCC 1847).

r.h: Touch me and see
set: It is still Easter evening. The two disciples have run back from Emmaus to Jerusalem and found the Eleven saying, “The Lord has risen indeed, and he has appeared to Simon!” (24:34). As they tell their story, Jesus himself appears. This is Luke’s last scene before the Ascension (24:50–53).
In Year B of the Lectionary this Gospel continues the Emmaus story. Luke is writing for readers who might think the risen Jesus was a vision or a ghost; he insists on the reality of the risen body.
str: v. 35: the Emmaus disciples tell how he was known in the breaking of the bread.
vv. 36–43: Jesus appears, shows his hands and feet, and eats.
vv. 44–47: he opens their minds to the Scriptures: suffering, resurrection, repentance for all nations.
v. 48: “You are witnesses.”
kw: Here a disembodied spirit or apparition. Jesus denies that he is one: he has flesh and bones.
A key word of Luke 24: the disciples’ eyes are opened (v. 31), the Scriptures are opened (v. 32), and their minds are opened (v. 45). The Risen One opens what was shut.
A change of mind and heart, a turning back to God. It is the first content of the mission, joined to the forgiveness of sins (v. 47).
vv: how he had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread.

“The breaking of the bread” is the name Luke uses in Acts for the Eucharist (Acts 2:42). The Catechism sees in the Emmaus journey the shape of the Mass: the word explained, then the bread broken (CCC 1347).
Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.

St Ignatius of Antioch, writing about AD 110, records a saying close to this, that the disciples should handle him and see that he was not a bodiless spirit, and stresses that the Lord was in the flesh after the Resurrection (in substance, Letter to the Smyrnaeans 3). The Catechism teaches that the risen body is the same body that was crucified, now glorified (CCC 645; CCC 999).
While in their joy they were disbelieving and still wondering,
An honest and tender note: the news is too good to believe. Joy itself makes them hesitate.
Then he opened their minds to understand the scriptures,
“The law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms” (v. 44) names the three parts of the Jewish Scriptures. The Resurrection fulfils the whole Old Testament (CCC 652).
You are witnesses of these things.
Not spectators but witnesses. In Acts 1:8 this becomes the program of the whole book: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth.
ch: The Church holds that the Resurrection was a real event in history, with manifestations that could be verified, and also more than a return to earthly life: the risen body is glorified and no longer bound by space and time (CCC 639; CCC 645–646). Luke 24 also shows how the risen Lord is met today: in the Scriptures opened and in the breaking of the bread, which is why every Mass has a Liturgy of the Word and a Liturgy of the Eucharist.

qa: Did the risen Jesus need to eat?

No. His glorified body did not need food. He ate to show that he was not a ghost but truly risen in the body. Peter later speaks of witnesses “who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10:41). The meal was a gift to their faith.
“You killed the Author of life”: does the Bible blame the Jewish people for the death of Jesus?

No. Peter speaks to a particular crowd in Jerusalem, as one of their own, calling them “friends” and offering forgiveness. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4), and the Catechism says that we sinners bear the graver responsibility (CCC 598).
What does “atoning sacrifice” mean? Was God angry and needing to be paid?

The Greek hilasmos means the means by which sin is taken away and communion restored. John says that the initiative is God’s: “he loved us and sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 4:10). The Catechism cites that verse to say that the Word became flesh to save us by reconciling us with God (CCC 457). The cross is God’s love reaching us, not a price wrung from him.
rite: This Sunday the Lectionary is in Year B, and the Gospel continues the Emmaus story with the appearance in Jerusalem. Through the Easter season the first reading comes from the Acts of the Apostles instead of the Old Testament, so that we watch the risen Lord at work in his Church. The Easter candle stands by the ambo or by the altar until Pentecost, and the Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus. Luke’s pairing of word and broken bread is the shape of every Mass, so this Sunday is a fitting one to teach the people why the Mass has two tables, the word and the altar.
study: Peter offers forgiveness to those who wronged his Lord. Whom do I need to forgive, or ask forgiveness of, this Easter?
1 John says we have an advocate. How does that change the way I go to confession?
Where do I most often meet the risen Lord: in the Scriptures, in the breaking of the bread, in others?
What is one way I can be a witness this week, in word or in deed?

lead: Stephen, one of the seven whose choosing we heard on Saturday, now steps forward: full of grace and power, he speaks with a wisdom his opponents cannot withstand, and when he is brought before the council his face is like the face of an angel. In the Gospel the crowd fed in Friday’s reading crosses the lake looking for Jesus, and he tells them to work for the food that endures for eternal life. The work God asks is to believe in the one he has sent. Psalm 119 blesses those who walk in the law of the Lord.

r.h: The face of an angel
set: Stephen was chosen to serve at table (6:5), but Luke now shows him as a powerful preacher and worker of signs. His opponents come from a synagogue of Greek-speaking Jews in Jerusalem. The “Freedmen” (Greek Libertinoi, from the Latin word) were probably Jews who had been slaves, or the descendants of slaves, freed in Rome or elsewhere; many think of the captives brought to Rome by Pompey in 63 BC. With them were Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia. Saul of Tarsus came from Cilicia; he will be present at Stephen’s death (7:58).
The dispute is among Jews in Jerusalem about the meaning of the temple and the Law in the light of Jesus. Luke shapes Stephen’s trial so that it recalls the trial of Jesus.
str: v. 8: Stephen’s grace and power.
vv. 9–10: debate, and wisdom his opponents cannot withstand.
vv. 11–14: secret instigation, a stirred crowd, arrest, false witnesses.
v. 15: the council sees his face like an angel’s.
kw: Luke says that the favour (charis) of God was upon the child Jesus (Luke 2:40), and that great power and great grace marked the apostles’ witness (Acts 4:33). Stephen, chosen for service, shares the same gifts.
The same charge as at Jesus’ trial, where false witnesses said that he would destroy the temple (Mark 14:56–58). The disciple walks his Master’s road.
The practices of the Law handed down from Moses. The accusation is that Stephen announces their end. In fact the first Christians in Jerusalem went on praying in the temple (2:46; 3:1).
vv: Stephen, full of grace and power, did great wonders and signs among the people.
The one chosen “to wait on tables” is the first, after the apostles, whom Luke shows working signs. Service and power go together.
But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.
Jesus had promised: “I will give you words and a wisdom that none of your opponents will be able to withstand or contradict” (Luke 21:15). The promise is kept in Stephen.
They set up false witnesses
When argument fails, some turn to falsehood. Luke presents this as the work of particular people, not of the Jewish people; many in Jerusalem had come to faith (6:7).
and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
Perhaps an echo of Moses, whose face shone after he spoke with God (Exodus 34:29). Stephen, accused of speaking against Moses, shines as Moses did.
ch: The Church honours Stephen as the first martyr, the protomartyr, and keeps his feast on 26 December, the day after Christmas, so that the birth of Christ is followed at once by the witness of blood. Luke tells his death as an echo of Jesus’ death: he commends his spirit to the Lord and prays for his persecutors (7:59–60).

r.h: The food that endures
set: This begins the long dialogue at Capernaum that will become the discourse on the Bread of Life, spoken in the synagogue there (6:59). The crowd fed on the far shore has noticed that Jesus did not leave in the disciples’ boat, and comes looking for him. Verses 22–24 are complicated, but their purpose is simple: to bring the same crowd face to face with Jesus again.
str: vv. 22–24: the crowd searches and crosses to Capernaum.
vv. 25–27: “When did you come here?”: Jesus answers with the true question, what they are seeking.
vv. 28–29: the work of God is to believe.
kw: Food in the sense of eating and nourishment. Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food that “endures”, a favourite word of John (menein, to remain, abide).
God the Father has set his seal on the Son of Man: he has marked him as his own and authorized him, as a seal authorizes a document.
The crowd asks about “works” in the plural, things to do. Jesus answers with one “work”: faith. Faith is both God’s work in us and our response.
vv: you are looking for me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.
They saw the bread but not what it signified. Jesus does not send them away; he tries to lead them from the gift to the Giver.
Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures for eternal life,
Not a contempt for daily bread, which Jesus himself teaches us to ask for. It is a question of what we live for.
This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.

St Augustine comments on these verses: “Believe, and you have eaten” (in substance, Tractates on John 25). Faith is the first way of receiving the Bread of Life; the Eucharist, which Jesus will speak of in 6:51–58, is received by faith.
ch: The Catechism teaches that faith is a gift of God, a supernatural virtue infused by him, and at the same time an authentically human act (CCC 153–154). John 6:29 holds both: it is “the work of God”, and it is something we are called to do. These verses prepare for the words that follow: “I am the bread of life” (6:35).

study: Stephen served tables and preached with wisdom. How might my ordinary service become a witness?
What am I really looking for when I seek Jesus? What “food that perishes” do I work hardest for?

lead: Acts reaches its first martyr, and the discourse at Capernaum goes on. Stephen, one of the Seven, whose arrest we heard of on Monday, ends his long speech before the council with hard prophetic words, sees heaven opened, and dies praying as Jesus prayed on the cross. In John the crowd asks for a sign like the manna, and Jesus answers that the true bread comes from his Father and that he himself is that bread. Psalm 31 gives Stephen’s last prayer its source: “Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit”.

r.h: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit
set: Stephen was one of the Seven chosen to serve the tables of the Greek-speaking widows (6:1–6), a man “full of grace and power” who also preached (6:8). Accused of speaking against the Temple and the law (6:13–14), he gave before the council the longest speech in Acts (7:2–53), retelling Israel’s story from Abraham to the Temple of Solomon. Today’s reading begins as the speech reaches its sharp end and the hearing turns into a killing.
Stephen speaks as a Jew to fellow Jews, in the voice of the prophets who rebuked their own people. Luke does not describe a formal sentence: the scene ends in a rush of anger outside the city.
str: vv. 51–53: Stephen’s rebuke: you resist the Spirit as your ancestors did.
vv. 54–56: their rage; his vision of the glory of God and of the Son of Man standing.
vv. 57–58: they drag him out and stone him; the witnesses lay their coats at the feet of Saul.
7:59–8:1a: two prayers, and death; Saul approves.
kw: The word God uses of Israel after the golden calf (Exodus 33:3, 5). Stephen takes it from the Torah itself: it is the language of a quarrel inside the family of the covenant, not an outsider’s insult.

Elsewhere the risen Christ is “seated” at the right hand of God (Psalm 110:1; Luke 22:69). Here he stands. Many interpreters see him rising to help and welcome his witness; others see him standing as witness and advocate in a court where Stephen is condemned.

Luke’s word for Stephen’s death (NRSV “he died”). Early Christians often spoke of death as sleep, because they awaited the resurrection (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). Our word “cemetery” comes from the same Greek family: a place of sleeping.
vv: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you are forever opposing the Holy Spirit, just as your ancestors used to do.

Hard words, but taken from Scripture (Leviticus 26:41; Jeremiah 6:10; 9:26). They are spoken to the members of the council at one hearing. The Church reads them as a warning to every hearer who resists the Spirit, never as a charge against the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
“Look,” he said, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”
This is the only place in Acts where Jesus is called the Son of Man. Stephen’s words echo what Jesus told the council at his own trial (Luke 22:69). What was promised there is seen here.
While they were stoning Stephen, he prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”

On the cross Jesus prayed to the Father, “into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46, from Psalm 31). Stephen makes the same prayer to Jesus. Within a few years of Easter, a Christian dies praying to Jesus as to God.
“Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he died.
Like Jesus in Luke 23:34, he prays for those who kill him. And he kneels, as Jesus knelt in the garden (Luke 22:41).
ch: The Church honours Stephen as the first martyr, the Protomartyr, and keeps his feast on 26 December, the day after Christmas: the Child born at Bethlehem is the Lord for whom his servant died. St Fulgentius of Ruspe, in a sermon the Church reads on that feast, says that the love which brought Christ down from heaven to earth raised Stephen from earth to heaven (in substance). The Catechism calls martyrdom “the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith” (CCC 2473) and teaches that Christian prayer reaches as far as the forgiveness of enemies (CCC 2844). St Augustine said that if Stephen had not prayed, the Church would not have had Paul (in substance). The young man at whose feet the coats were laid would soon be called.

r.h: My Father gives you the true bread from heaven
set: After the feeding of the five thousand (6:1–15) and the walking on the sea (6:16–21), the crowd finds Jesus again at Capernaum (6:24–25). He has told them to work for the food that endures for eternal life, and that the work of God is to believe in the one whom he has sent (6:27–29). Now they ask for proof. They have eaten bread in the wilderness; they want manna, the sign of Moses. John notes that the Passover, the feast of the Exodus, was near (6:4).
str: vv. 30–31: the crowd asks for a sign and recalls the manna.
vv. 32–33: Jesus corrects them: not Moses but my Father; not only in the past but now (“gives”); the bread that comes down and gives life to the world.
v. 34: “Sir, give us this bread always.”
v. 35: “I am the bread of life.”
kw: John’s word for the miracles of Jesus: deeds that point beyond themselves. The crowd has just seen one and asks for another. The sign they need is the person standing before them.
In John alēthinos means real, the thing itself to which earlier gifts pointed: the true light (1:9), the true vine (15:1). The manna was a real gift of God; it was also a sign of a greater one.
The first of the sayings in John where Jesus says “I am” with an image: bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine. Behind the words many hear the name God revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14).
vv: Our ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’”

The quotation gathers Exodus 16:4, 15 and Psalm 78:24. A Jewish writing from about the same period hoped that the treasury of manna would come down again in the days of the Messiah (2 Baruch 29:8), and the crowd may share that hope.
it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is my Father who gives you the true bread from heaven.
Two corrections in one sentence: the giver is God, not Moses, and the giving is now, not only long ago.
“Sir, give us this bread always.”
The Samaritan woman said almost the same about water (4:15). Both misunderstand at first, and both are led further.
“I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.
Coming and believing are one movement here. Bread and drink together already point toward the meal Jesus will speak of later in the chapter.
ch: The Catechism notes that while the other Gospels and St Paul hand on the institution of the Eucharist, St John reports the words at Capernaum that prepare for it: Christ calls himself the bread of life, come down from heaven (CCC 1338). It also recalls that the manna in the desert always reminded Israel that it lives by the bread of the Word of God (CCC 1334). Many commentators see two movements in the discourse: in the first, Jesus is the bread received by faith, in his word and person; from verse 51 the language becomes plainly eucharistic. The Church does not set the two against each other. At every Mass we are fed from the one table of the Word of God and of the Body of Christ (Dei Verbum 21).

qa: Why does Stephen speak so harshly to his own people?

He speaks as an Israelite within Israel, using the words of Moses and the prophets, who also rebuked their own generation. His last words are a prayer for forgiveness. The Church teaches that the Jews are not to be presented as rejected or accursed (Nostra Aetate 4), and that all sinners share the responsibility for the Passion (CCC 598).
study: Stephen prayed for those who were killing him. Whom do I find it hardest to pray for, and can I name that person to the Lord today?
Like the crowd, do I ask God for signs when he has already given me himself in his word and in the Eucharist?

lead: Stephen’s death does not silence the word; it scatters it. The reading from Acts begins in the same verse where Tuesday’s ended: a persecution, in which Saul took a leading part, drives the believers out of Jerusalem, and Philip brings the Gospel to Samaria, where “there was great joy in that city”. In the Gospel the discourse at Capernaum continues: the will of the Father is that nothing given to the Son should be lost. Psalm 66 calls all the earth to cry out to God with joy.

r.h: Those who were scattered proclaimed the word
set: Devout men bury Stephen with loud lamentation, and a severe persecution falls on the church in Jerusalem. Many scholars think it struck above all the Greek-speaking believers of Stephen’s circle, since the apostles were able to stay in the city. Philip, named next after Stephen in the list of the Seven (6:5), is not the apostle Philip.

Acts follows the plan announced by the risen Lord: “in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (1:8). With this reading the Gospel reaches Samaria. Jews and Samaritans had long been divided over worship and the Temple (John 4:9, 20), and the Samaritans too awaited one who was to come (John 4:25).
str: vv. 1b–3: persecution; Stephen’s burial; Saul ravages the church.
v. 4: the scattered believers proclaim the word.
vv. 5–8: Philip in Samaria: preaching, signs, healing and joy.
kw: The verb is built on speirō, “to sow”, the root of our word “diaspora”. What was meant to destroy the community sows it across the land.
A strong word, used of wild animals mauling or of an army laying waste. Paul himself later admits that he was violently persecuting the church of God (Galatians 1:13).
A mark of Luke’s writing, from the angels at Bethlehem (Luke 2:10) to the end of Acts. Here the joy belongs to a whole city of Samaritans.
vv: Now those who were scattered went from place to place, proclaiming the word.
Not the apostles but ordinary believers, refugees, are the first missionaries beyond Jerusalem.
Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah to them.

Some ancient manuscripts read “the city”, others “a city”, and translations differ. If “the city” is meant, it may be the old capital, rebuilt by Herod the Great as Sebaste. Philip proclaims “the Messiah”: the Christ Samaria too was waiting for.
So there was great joy in that city.
The last words of the reading. Healing of body and spirit, together with the good news, bring joy.
ch: Tertullian wrote at the end of the second century that the blood of Christians is seed (in substance). Acts already shows the pattern: suffering does not end the mission; it carries it further. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the pilgrim Church is missionary by its very nature (Ad Gentes 2). Philip, counted by tradition among the first deacons and later called “the evangelist” (21:8), shows that the work of proclaiming belongs to more than the apostles. The Catechism adds that the Church on mission walks the road Christ walked, the way of poverty and obedience, of service and self-sacrifice even to death (CCC 852).

r.h: I will never drive away anyone who comes to me
set: The discourse at Capernaum continues. Verse 35 repeats the last line of Tuesday’s Gospel, “I am the bread of life”, and Jesus now speaks of the will of his Father. The crowd has seen him and yet does not believe (v. 36). Jesus answers, not with a new sign, but with a promise about all who come to him.
str: v. 35: the bread of life.
v. 36: seeing without believing.
vv. 37–38: all that the Father gives will come; I will never drive them away; I came to do the will of the one who sent me.
vv. 39–40: the Father’s will: lose nothing, eternal life, “I will raise them up on the last day”.
kw: The word comes four times in vv. 38–40. Jesus said that his food is to do the will of the one who sent him (4:34); here we learn what that will is: that none be lost.
A strong double negative in Greek. In chapter 9 the man born blind will be driven out (9:34); whoever comes to Jesus is never driven out.
“I will raise them up on the last day” comes four times in this chapter (vv. 39, 40, 44, 54). The bread of life leads to the resurrection of the body.
vv: Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and anyone who comes to me I will never drive away;
God’s gift and our coming are held together. No one who comes is turned back, however late or however wounded.
for I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.
The Catechism quotes this verse in speaking of the whole life of Jesus as an offering to the Father, which leads him to the cross (CCC 606).
This is indeed the will of my Father, that all who see the Son and believe in him may have eternal life; and I will raise them up on the last day.”
Eternal life begins now, in believing; it is completed in the resurrection.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: it is he who on the last day will raise up those who have believed in him and who have eaten his body and drunk his blood (CCC 994). John 6:37–40 is one of the Gospels the Church offers for funeral Masses: at the grave the Church leans on the promise that the Son loses nothing the Father has given him.

study: When has a loss or a hardship in my life become, like the scattering in Acts, an opening for the Gospel?
Jesus says he will never drive away anyone who comes to him. Is there someone I keep at a distance whom he would welcome?

lead: Two readings about how people come to Christ. On the desert road to Gaza a royal official from the far south is reading Isaiah without understanding, and the Spirit sends Philip to run beside his chariot. In John, Jesus says that no one can come to him unless drawn by the Father, and then the discourse takes its decisive turn: “the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh”. Psalm 66 sounds like the official’s own voice on his way home: “Come and hear, all you who fear God, and I will tell what he has done for me.”

r.h: Do you understand what you are reading?
set: Philip has been preaching in Samaria. An angel now sends him south, to the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza, the old route toward Egypt. There he meets a man Luke calls an Ethiopian. In the Bible “Ethiopia” (Hebrew Kush) means the land south of Egypt on the upper Nile, the kingdom of Meroë in today’s Sudan, rather than modern Ethiopia. “Candace” was the title of its ruling queens, not a personal name. For Greeks and Romans this was the edge of the known world.

The man is a eunuch and a high official, and he has been to Jerusalem to worship. The law of Deuteronomy 23:1 kept such a man out of the assembly, but Isaiah 56:3–5 promised eunuchs “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters”. Luke does not say whether he was a convert or a God-fearing Gentile; the story is told before the baptism of Cornelius (Acts 10).
str: vv. 26–29: the angel and the Spirit send Philip to the chariot.
vv. 30–35: “Do you understand?” Isaiah 53 and the good news about Jesus.
vv. 36–38: “Here is water!” The baptism.
vv. 39–40: Philip is taken away; the eunuch goes on rejoicing; Philip preaches as far as Caesarea.
kw: “How can I, unless someone guides me?” The same verb is used of the Spirit who “will guide you into all the truth” (John 16:13). Scripture is read best with a guide, within the Church.
Starting from Isaiah, Philip “proclaimed to him the good news about Jesus”. As on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:27), the risen Christ is the key to the Scriptures.

The same verb returns when Peter asks whether anyone can withhold the water of baptism from Cornelius’ household (10:47), and when he says he could not hinder God (11:17). Some scholars think it echoes a question asked at early baptisms.
vv: So Philip ran up to it and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah. He asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
In the ancient world people usually read aloud, so Philip can hear him. The Greek has a play on words: ginōskeis ha anaginōskeis, “do you know what you are reading?”
“Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth.
Isaiah 53:7–8, in the Greek translation the official would have been reading. It is the fourth Servant Song, read every Good Friday.
The eunuch asked Philip, “About whom, may I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?”
The question is still asked today. Christians answer with Philip: the Servant’s silent suffering is fulfilled in Jesus.
“Look, here is water! What is to prevent me from being baptized?”

Many later manuscripts add a verse 37 in which Philip asks for faith and the eunuch replies, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.” The best ancient manuscripts lack it, so the NRSV passes from verse 36 to verse 38. The addition shows how early the Church joined baptism to a profession of faith.
the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.
Philip disappears; the joy remains.
ch: St Irenaeus in the second century says that this man was sent into the regions of Ethiopia to preach what he himself had believed (in substance), and many Christians of Africa look to him as a forerunner of their faith. St Jerome, writing about the study of Scripture, points to him: he held the book but did not understand it until a guide came (in substance). The Second Vatican Council teaches that Scripture must be read in the same Spirit in which it was written, with attention to the living Tradition of the whole Church (Dei Verbum 12; CCC 111–113). The Catechism also notes that from the day of Pentecost the Church has celebrated and administered holy Baptism (CCC 1226).

r.h: The living bread that came down from heaven
set: The hearers, whom John here calls “the Jews”, complain because Jesus, whose father and mother they think they know, says that he has come down from heaven (6:41–42). In John 6 the term refers to the Galilean listeners in the synagogue at Capernaum (6:59), not to the Jewish people as such. Their murmuring recalls Israel’s murmuring over food in the desert (Exodus 16:2). Jesus answers that faith is a gift of the Father, and then speaks of a bread that is his flesh.
str: vv. 44–46: no one comes unless drawn by the Father; “they shall all be taught by God”.
v. 47: whoever believes has eternal life.
vv. 48–50: the bread of life and the manna: the ancestors died, this bread gives life.
v. 51: the living bread; the bread is “my flesh”, given for the life of the world.
kw: A strong verb, used of hauling in a net (21:6, 11). Jesus uses it again: “I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (12:32). The Father’s drawing does not force; it attracts.
From Isaiah 54:13, a promise for the restored Jerusalem. Faith is more than learning from human teachers: God himself teaches the heart.

The word of the Prologue: “the Word became flesh” (1:14). In verse 51 Jesus no longer speaks only of bread from heaven but of his own flesh, given “for the life of the world”, words that point to the cross and to the Eucharist.
vv: No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me; and I will raise that person up on the last day.
This does not mean that God refuses some. It means that faith is first God’s work in us; no one reaches Christ by human power alone (CCC 153).
Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.
The manna was a true gift, but it fed a mortal life. The bread Jesus gives feeds a life that death does not end.
I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread will live forever; and the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”
“I will give” is future, and “for” (hyper) is the word used of Christ’s sacrifice (compare Luke 22:19, “given for you”). The gift will be made on the cross and given at the table.
ch: St Augustine, commenting on “unless drawn by the Father”, says that we are drawn not by force but by delight, as a sheep is drawn by the green branch held out to it; he even quotes the poet Virgil, that each one is drawn by his own delight (in substance). The Catechism teaches that faith is a gift of God and at the same time a truly human act (CCC 153–155). In verse 51 the Church hears the Eucharist announced: the bread is the flesh of the Lord given for the life of the world (CCC 1338, 1406).

qa: If no one can come unless the Father draws him, are some people left out?

No. Jesus also says that, lifted up on the cross, he will draw all people to himself (12:32), and God desires everyone to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4). God predestines no one to be lost (CCC 1037). His drawing is offered to all, and it respects our freedom, which can accept or refuse it (CCC 1730).
study: Who has been a “Philip” for me, helping me understand the Scriptures? For whom could I be one?
What draws me to Christ today, and what in my life might make it harder for others to be drawn to him?

lead: Friday brings the turning point of Saul’s life on the Damascus road, and the most direct words of the discourse at Capernaum: “my flesh is true food and my blood is true drink”. The two readings meet in one truth. Christ so joins himself to his own that to persecute them is to persecute him, and to eat his flesh is to abide in him. Psalm 117, the shortest psalm, sends us out: “Go out to all the world and tell the Good News”.

r.h: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
set: Saul of Tarsus was a Jew of the dispersion and a Pharisee, educated in Jerusalem (22:3; Philippians 3:5). He approved of Stephen’s death (8:1) and now asks the high priest for letters to the synagogues of Damascus, so as to bring back bound any who belong to “the Way”. Acts tells his conversion three times (here, 22:6–16 and 26:12–18), a sign of how much it mattered to Luke. Paul himself speaks of it briefly: God “was pleased to reveal his Son to me” (Galatians 1:15–16).

Many scholars prefer to speak of a call rather than a conversion, because Paul describes it in words that recall the call of Jeremiah (Galatians 1:15; Jeremiah 1:5). He did not leave the God of Israel; he came to know Jesus as Israel’s Messiah and Lord.
str: vv. 1–2: Saul sets out for Damascus.
vv. 3–9: light from heaven; “Saul, Saul”; three days without sight, food or drink.
vv. 10–16: the Lord sends Ananias, who protests and is answered.
vv. 17–20: “Brother Saul”; sight, baptism, food, and preaching that Jesus is the Son of God.
kw: One of the earliest names for the Christian movement in Acts (9:2; 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). Jesus had called himself the way (John 14:6).
an instrument whom I have chosen

Literally “a vessel of choice”, a chosen container or tool. Paul later says that we have this treasure in clay jars (2 Corinthians 4:7). The vessel is chosen for what it will carry: the name of Jesus.
Ananias’ greeting to the persecutor. Before the scales fall from Saul’s eyes, he has been received into a family.
vv: He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
Not “my disciples”, but “me”. The risen Christ is one with his followers.
He asked, “Who are you, Lord?” The reply came, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
Paul’s whole later teaching on the Church as the body of Christ is folded into this answer.
But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem;
Ananias is honest with the Lord. Obedience does not need to hide fear; it needs to go anyway.
But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is an instrument whom I have chosen to bring my name before Gentiles and kings and before the people of Israel;
The plan of Paul’s mission as Acts will tell it: Gentiles, kings and governors (Felix, Festus, Agrippa), and his own people, to whom he usually went first.
ch: St Augustine, preaching on the Ascension, says that Christ in heaven cried out on behalf of his body on earth: he did not say “why do you persecute my saints?” but “why do you persecute me?” (in substance). The Catechism teaches that Christ and his Church together make up the “whole Christ” (CCC 795). The Roman calendar keeps the Conversion of St Paul as a feast on 25 January. Ananias, of whom we know almost nothing else, reminds us that the Lord often works through simple disciples who are willing to knock on a dangerous door.

r.h: My flesh is true food
set: The hearers now argue among themselves: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” The question is serious, and Jesus does not soften his words; he repeats them more strongly. John closes the discourse by naming its place: the synagogue at Capernaum (v. 59). In this chapter “the Jews” are the Galileans in that synagogue, not the Jewish people as such.
str: v. 52: the dispute.
vv. 53–54: unless you eat and drink, you have no life; whoever eats has eternal life and will be raised.
vv. 55–57: true food and true drink; abiding; life from the Father, through the Son, to the one who eats.
vv. 58–59: this bread and the manna; the place.
kw: From verse 54 John changes from the usual verb for eating to trōgō, a more physical word, used for chewing or munching. Many commentators see in this a refusal to let the words be taken as a mere figure.
Not a picture of food but real food. Jesus answers the question “how can this man give us his flesh?” by saying that he will.
A favourite word of John. In the Eucharist Christ and the believer dwell in one another, as the branch abides in the vine (15:4).
vv: “Very truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.
For Jewish hearers the drinking of blood was forbidden (Leviticus 17:10–14), so these words were truly shocking. Jesus does not explain them away.
for my flesh is true food and my blood is true drink.
The Church reads this verse as one of the plainest witnesses to the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist (CCC 1374, 1406).
Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them.
The Catechism quotes this verse: Holy Communion deepens our union with Christ (CCC 1391).
Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me.
A chain of life: from the Father to the Son, from the Son to us.
ch: Early in the second century St Ignatius of Antioch called the Eucharist “the medicine of immortality” (Letter to the Ephesians 20), and wrote that some kept away from it because they would not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 7). The Catechism places the words of John 6 at the centre of its teaching on the Eucharist (CCC 1338, 1406). Following St Paul VI, it explains that this presence is called “real” not to deny Christ’s other ways of being present, but because it is presence in the fullest sense (CCC 1374).

qa: Did Jesus mean his words only as a symbol?

If he had, it would have been easy to say so when many disciples left him (6:66). Instead he repeated them more strongly. From the earliest Fathers the Church has believed that the Eucharist is truly his Body and Blood, while the manner of this presence is a mystery that the senses cannot grasp and faith receives (CCC 1376, 1381).
study: Jesus says to Saul, “why do you persecute me?” How does it change the way I treat others to know that Christ is one with them?
How can I prepare more carefully for Holy Communion this Sunday, knowing that in it I abide in Christ and he in me?

lead: The week closes with two scenes of Peter. In Acts he goes about among the believers of a Church that now has peace, and through his word the Lord raises up a paralysed man at Lydda and a beloved disciple at Joppa. In John, when many disciples leave after the hard words about his flesh and blood, Peter answers for the Twelve: “Lord, to whom can we go?” Psalm 116 gives the grateful question: “How shall I make a return to the Lord for all the good he has done for me?”

r.h: Tabitha, get up
set: After Saul’s conversion Luke pauses with a summary: the church in Judea, Galilee and Samaria has peace and grows (v. 31). Then he returns to Peter, who visits the believers on the coastal plain. Lydda (today Lod) lies inland from Joppa (today Jaffa), the old port of Jerusalem. These visits lead to Peter’s stay in Joppa (9:43) and to his call to the house of Cornelius in the next chapter.
str: v. 31: summary: the church at peace and growing.
vv. 32–35: Aeneas healed at Lydda; many turn to the Lord.
vv. 36–39: Tabitha dies at Joppa; the disciples send for Peter; the widows weep.
vv. 40–42: Peter prays; “Tabitha, get up”; many believe.
kw: Verse 31 uses the word in the singular for the believers of three regions together: already one Church in many places. Some later manuscripts have the plural “churches”.
“Jesus Christ heals you.” Peter does not say “I heal you”. As at the Temple gate (3:6), the name of Jesus does the work.
The feminine form of “disciple” occurs only here in the New Testament. Tabitha is the Aramaic word for a gazelle; Dorcas is the same word in Greek.
vv: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; get up and make your bed!” And immediately he got up.
As Jesus told a paralysed man to take up his bed (Luke 5:24), so Peter speaks in his name.
She was devoted to good works and acts of charity.
Literally “full of good works and of almsgiving”. Her holiness was made of needles and cloth.
All the widows stood beside him, weeping and showing tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was with them.
Widows were among the poorest in that society. Their grief is her best eulogy: they show what she made for them.
Peter put all of them outside, and then he knelt down and prayed. He turned to the body and said, “Tabitha, get up.”

The scene recalls the raising of Jairus’ daughter, where Jesus put the mourners outside and said, “Talitha cum”, “Little girl, get up!” (Mark 5:40–41). In Greek the two words differ by a single letter. But unlike Jesus, Peter first kneels and prays: the power is not his own.
ch: The Church sees in Tabitha a model of charity done with the hands, and many sewing circles for the poor have taken the name of Dorcas. The Catechism counts clothing the naked among the corporal works of mercy (CCC 2447). The raising of Tabitha also shows what Easter means for the Church: the risen Lord goes on working through his apostles and confirms their word by signs (Mark 16:20).

r.h: Lord, to whom can we go?
set: The discourse is over, and now the disciples react. Not only the crowd but “many of his disciples” find the teaching too hard. John records the first great falling away, and the first confession of the Twelve in his Gospel. It is his counterpart to Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi in the other Gospels (Mark 8:29).
str: vv. 60–61: “This teaching is difficult.”
vv. 62–65: the Son of Man ascending; the spirit gives life; no one comes unless it is granted by the Father.
v. 66: many turn back.
vv. 67–69: “Do you also wish to go away?” Peter’s answer.
kw: Not hard to understand but hard to accept. They understood well enough that he meant what he said.
“Flesh” here means human nature left to itself, judging by its own lights, as in 3:6. It does not cancel what Jesus said of his own flesh in vv. 51–56. His words are “spirit and life”.
A rare title (Mark 1:24). Some later manuscripts change it to “the Christ, the Son of the living God”, under the influence of Matthew 16:16; most scholars hold the shorter reading to be the original.
vv: When many of his disciples heard it, they said, “This teaching is difficult; who can accept it?”
The Catechism notes that the first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the announcement of the Passion scandalized them (CCC 1336).
It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh is useless. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.

St Augustine explains that the hearers took the flesh as meat cut up in the market, and that this was the useless way to understand him; the flesh of Christ, joined to the Spirit, gives life (in substance).
Because of this many of his disciples turned back and no longer went about with him.
Jesus lets them go. He does not change the teaching to keep the crowd.
Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.
Peter does not claim to understand everything. He has found no one else with words like these. His faith rests on a person.
ch: The Catechism takes up the question of verse 67: it echoes through the ages as a loving invitation to discover that only he has the words of eternal life, and that to receive the gift of the Eucharist in faith is to receive the Lord himself (CCC 1336). Peter’s answer has become the prayer of every Christian who struggles with the faith and yet stays.

qa: What should I do when a teaching of the Church seems too hard to accept?

Do what Peter did: stay close to Jesus, and say honestly that you are still learning. Ask, read, pray, and talk with a priest or catechist. The Catechism, quoting St John Henry Newman, reminds us that ten thousand difficulties do not make one doubt (CCC 157).
study: Tabitha’s holiness was seen in the clothes she made for widows. What ordinary work of my hands could become a work of mercy this week?
When have I been tempted to “go away”, and what has kept me, like Peter, with the Lord?

lead: The Fourth Sunday of Easter is Good Shepherd Sunday. Each year its Gospel comes from John 10, and this year Jesus speaks the central sentence: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” Around it the other readings show who this shepherd is. In Acts, Peter on trial before the council says that there is salvation in no other name. Psalm 118 sings of the stone the builders rejected, the verse Peter has just quoted. The First Letter of John tells us what the shepherd’s self-giving has made of us: “we are God’s children now”.
The key words today are name, stone, children and lay down. The shepherd lays down his life of his own accord and takes it up again; that is why this Sunday belongs to Easter.

r.h: No other name
set: Peter and John had healed a man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate of the Temple “in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth” (3:2–6). A crowd gathered and Peter preached. Then the priests, the captain of the Temple and the Sadducees, who did not accept the resurrection of the dead, arrested them (4:1–3). The next day they stand before the council, with Annas and Caiaphas, the men who had handed Jesus over a few weeks earlier (4:5–6). The question put to them is: “By what power or by what name did you do this?” (4:7).

Jesus had promised that when his disciples were brought before rulers, the Holy Spirit would teach them what to say (Luke 12:11–12). Peter, who had denied Jesus before a servant girl in the high priest’s courtyard, now speaks before the high priest himself.
str: v. 8a: Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit.
vv. 8b–10: the healing was done by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, crucified and raised by God.
v. 11: Psalm 118:22 fulfilled: the rejected stone.
v. 12: there is salvation in no other name.
kw: The word of the trial: the council asks “by what name?” and Peter answers with the name of Jesus. In the Bible a name stands for the person and his power. The name “Jesus” means “God saves” (CCC 430).
In v. 9 the word translated “healed” is the verb “to save”, and in v. 12 its noun, “salvation”. With one Greek word family Peter moves from one man’s healing to the salvation of all.

Peter quotes Psalm 118:22 with small changes. Where the Greek psalm says “rejected”, he uses a sharper word, “treated as nothing”, and adds “by you, the builders”. The builders are the leaders in front of him.
vv: Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders,
Courage here is a gift, not a matter of temperament. The same Peter was afraid beside a charcoal fire (John 18:17–18).
if we are questioned today because of a good deed done to someone who was sick
A touch of irony: they are on trial for an act of kindness.
by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead.

“You” are the members of the council, the rulers who had handed Jesus over. This is not a charge against the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). As always in Acts, the weight falls on what God did: “whom God raised”.
There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among mortals by which we must be saved.”
“Given” by God: the name is a gift, not a human achievement. “Must” means that this is the way God has chosen.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse in its teaching on the name of Jesus: the divine name that alone brings salvation is present in the person of the Son, and from now on all may call upon it (CCC 432). The declaration Dominus Iesus (2000) builds on it in teaching that Jesus Christ is the one and universal Saviour. The Church also teaches that his grace reaches, in ways known to God, those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel but seek God with a sincere heart (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847).

r.h: The stone the builders rejected
set: Psalm 118 is a song of thanksgiving, sung in procession to the Temple by one whom God has rescued from mortal danger. It closes the Hallel (Psalms 113–118), sung at the great feasts and at Passover. Today the Church sings it because Peter has just quoted it before the council: the psalm becomes the answer of the whole assembly to his words.
str: v. 1: give thanks, for his steadfast love endures forever.
vv. 8–9: better to take refuge in the Lord than to trust in mortals or princes.
vv. 21–23: you answered me; the rejected stone has become the cornerstone.
vv. 26, 28–29: blessed is the one who comes; you are my God; give thanks.
kw: To shelter under someone, as under a rock or under wings. The psalm sets this trust against trust in “princes”, which fits a day when Peter stands before rulers and does not fear them.
the stone that the builders rejected
A stone thrown aside as unfit, then set at the head of the corner. Jesus applied it to himself (Mark 12:10–11), and both Peter in Acts and 1 Peter 2:7 take it up.
blessed is the one who comes
The greeting for pilgrims arriving at the Temple. The crowds greeted Jesus with it as he entered Jerusalem (Mark 11:9), and the Church sings it at every Mass within the Holy, Holy, Holy.
vv: It is better to take refuge in the Lord than to put confidence in princes.
Peter and John had no protector among the powerful. Their refuge was the Lord.
The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone. This is the Lord’s doing; it is marvelous in our eyes.

The Christian reading does not take the psalm away from Israel. It sees in Israel’s festival song the pattern of the cross and the Resurrection, and it gives the credit where the psalm gives it: “the Lord’s doing”.
Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.
On Palm Sunday these words greeted the shepherd going to lay down his life. At Mass they greet him as he comes to us on the altar.
ch: The early Church found in this psalm one of its clearest prophecies of the Resurrection, and the New Testament quotes verse 22 several times (Mark 12:10; Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7; compare Ephesians 2:20). In the Roman liturgy it is the psalm of Easter Day and is heard often through the Easter season. Christ is the cornerstone on which the Church is built (CCC 756).

r.h: We are God’s children now
set: The First Letter of John was written, probably near the end of the first century, to communities formed by the Gospel of John. Tradition attributes it to St John the Apostle; many scholars think it comes from a disciple or a circle close to him, sharing the Gospel’s language of light, love, truth and abiding. Some members had left the community (2:19), and the letter reassures those who remain about who they are before God.
str: v. 1a: see what love the Father has given us: we are called children of God, and we are.
v. 1b: why the world does not know us.
v. 2: we are children now; what we will be is not yet revealed; we will be like him and see him as he is.
kw: The word means “of what kind”, and it once meant “from what country”: a love so unusual that it seems to come from somewhere else.

Not only a title. The letter adds at once, “and that is what we are”. Those words, kai esmen in Greek, are missing in some late manuscripts and so in the King James Version, but the ancient witnesses have them.
Used twice in verse 2: what we will be has not yet been revealed; when he is revealed. Our future is hidden in his coming.
vv: See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God; and that is what we are.
We are children by adoption, through the only Son. Baptism makes us adopted children of God and members of Christ (CCC 1265).
The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know him.
“The world” in John’s writings often means human life organized without God. Christians should not be surprised to be misunderstood.
Beloved, we are God’s children now; what we will be has not yet been revealed.
Now and not yet: the shape of Christian hope in one sentence.
What we do know is this: when he is revealed, we will be like him, for we will see him as he is.
The Catechism quotes this verse in speaking of heaven, where the blessed see God face to face (CCC 1023), and calls this contemplation the beatific vision (CCC 1028).
ch: St Augustine, preaching on this letter, says that the whole life of a good Christian is a holy desire: we do not yet see, but by longing we are stretched so that we may be filled when he comes (in substance). The letter itself joins the gift to the task: all who have this hope in him purify themselves, as he is pure (3:3). Being God’s child is not a reward for good behaviour; good behaviour is the family likeness that grace slowly forms in us.

r.h: The good shepherd lays down his life
set: Jesus speaks these words in Jerusalem after healing the man born blind, whom some of the leaders then drove out (John 9). The background is Ezekiel 34, where God rebukes the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises: “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep” (Ezekiel 34:15) and “I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David” (34:23). In Israel God himself is the shepherd (Psalm 23), and David the shepherd-king is the model of the king to come. Jesus claims both promises.
str: vv. 11–13: the good shepherd and the hired hand.
vv. 14–15: mutual knowledge, as between the Father and the Son; he lays down his life.
v. 16: other sheep; one flock, one shepherd.
vv. 17–18: he lays down his life of his own accord, to take it up again; the Father’s command.
kw: Kalos means good in the sense of noble and beautiful, good as a thing should be. He is not only kind; he is the true shepherd, the model of every shepherd.

The verb “lay down” comes five times in these verses. It is the same verb John uses when Jesus lays aside his garments to wash the disciples’ feet (13:4): the shepherd gives up his life as one lays down a cloak.
A man paid by the day. The sheep are not his, so he does not risk himself for them. The contrast is between love and self-interest.
vv: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
Ordinary shepherds risked their lives against lions and bears (1 Samuel 17:34–35). This shepherd gives his. The death of the shepherd is the life of the flock.
I know my own and my own know me, just as the Father knows me and I know the Father.
In the Bible “to know” is to love and to be bound together. The bond between Jesus and his own is drawn into the bond between the Son and the Father.
I have other sheep that do not belong to this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd.
The other sheep are above all the Gentiles who will believe. The Latin Vulgate wrote “one fold”, but the Greek says “one flock”: the unity is in the one shepherd whose voice all hear.
No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again.
The Catechism quotes these words to show the sovereign freedom of the Son of God as he went to his death (CCC 609). The Resurrection is the second half of the same act of love.
ch: The Good Shepherd is one of the oldest images in Christian art: in the Roman catacombs he appears as a young shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders. St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, warns that a pastor can flee without moving a step, by keeping silent when he sees the wolf come (in substance). The Catechism describes the Church as a sheepfold whose one gate is Christ, and as a flock which, though governed by human shepherds, is unfailingly led and nourished by Christ himself, the Good Shepherd (CCC 754). The Second Vatican Council asks every bishop to keep before his eyes the example of the Good Shepherd (Lumen Gentium 27).

qa: Does “no other name” mean that only Christians can be saved?

No one is saved except through Christ, the one mediator between God and humankind (1 Timothy 2:5; CCC 846). The Church also teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ and his Church, yet seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will as their conscience shows it, can attain salvation (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). Their salvation too comes from Christ, by grace. This is why the Church remains missionary (CCC 848).
Who are the “other sheep” of John 10:16?

Most Fathers and commentators understand them as the Gentiles, who were not of the fold of Israel and would be gathered through the preaching of the apostles, as Acts shows. The verse is also read as a call to pray and work for the unity of all Christians, so that there may be one flock under one shepherd.
Why is this Sunday a day of prayer for vocations?

Since 1964, when it was first kept at the call of St Paul VI, the Church has kept the World Day of Prayer for Vocations on Good Shepherd Sunday. The Lord himself told us to ask the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into his harvest (Matthew 9:38). Every vocation, to the priesthood, to consecrated life or to marriage, is a share in the shepherd’s self-giving.
rite: Today is the World Day of Prayer for Vocations, which St Paul VI instituted and which was first kept in 1964; the Pope usually publishes a message for it. The Collect of the day asks that the humble flock may reach where the brave Shepherd has gone before (in substance). In many parishes priests and religious speak of their call, and families are asked to pray for vocations. It is a good Sunday to pray by name for the priests who baptized, taught and absolved you, and for the young people of your parish.
study: Peter says there is no other name by which we must be saved. How do I speak of Jesus, gently and clearly, to someone of another faith or of none?
What “rejected stone” in my parish or family might God be choosing to build upon?
John says “we are God’s children now”. Where do I most need to believe this about myself, and about someone I find hard to love?
The good shepherd lays down his life; the hired hand runs away. In my own responsibilities at home, at work or in the parish, when am I tempted to act like a hired hand?

lead: Both readings are about a door. In Jerusalem Peter explains why he went through the door of a Gentile house, and the believers end by praising God: “Then God has given even to the Gentiles the repentance that leads to life.” In John, Jesus calls himself the gate through which the sheep come in and go out and find pasture. Sunday’s Gospel heard the Good Shepherd lay down his life (John 10:11–18); today the Church goes back to the opening of the same discourse. Psalms 42–43 sing the thirst for the living God that only this gate satisfies.

r.h: Who was I that I could hinder God?
set: News travels faster than Peter. Before he is back in Jerusalem, the believers in Judea have heard that the Gentiles have accepted the word of God (10:1–48). Some Jewish believers are troubled, not about the baptism itself but because Peter ate with uncircumcised men (11:3). Table fellowship was where the Law’s distinction between clean and unclean was most visible. Peter does not argue from theory; he tells what happened, “step by step”. Luke tells the story of Cornelius a second time here, and recalls it again in 15:7–9, a sign of how much it matters to him.
str: vv. 1–3: the news and the complaint.
vv. 4–10: the vision at Joppa, three times over.
vv. 11–14: the three men, the Spirit’s command, the angel’s message to Cornelius.
vv. 15–17: the Spirit falls “just as it had upon us”.
v. 18: silence, then praise.
kw: to make a distinction, to take issue

Luke plays on one verb. In v. 2 the believers “criticized” Peter (diekrinonto); in v. 12 the Spirit tells him to go with the men “not to make a distinction” (mēden diakrinanta). Those who were dividing are taught by the Spirit not to divide. Some manuscripts have a related form meaning “without hesitating”, which is how the Malayalam POC renders the verse.

The same verb sounds at the baptism of the Ethiopian (8:36) and in Cornelius’ house (10:47). Some scholars hear in it an echo of an early baptismal question. Here Peter’s answer is final: no one may hinder what God has given.
Literally a change of mind and heart. The Jerusalem believers call it a gift: God “has given” it. Conversion is first God’s work in a person, and then that person’s answer.
vv: What God has made clean, you must not call profane.
The voice is not about food alone. In Cornelius’ house Peter himself drew the conclusion: God had shown him that he should not call anyone profane or unclean (10:28).
the Holy Spirit fell upon them just as it had upon us at the beginning.
“At the beginning” points to Pentecost. Peter sees in Cornelius’ house a Pentecost of the Gentiles: the same Spirit, the same gift, and no second class of believers.
who was I that I could hinder God?
Peter’s authority shows itself here as obedience. He does not open the door by his own decision; he recognizes a door God has already opened.
Then God has given even to the Gentiles the repentance that leads to life.
The word “even” carries all the surprise. The Gentiles are not taking Israel’s place; they are welcomed into the blessing promised to Abraham for all the families of the earth (Genesis 12:3).
ch: The Church reads this chapter as the moment when the mission to all nations was accepted in Jerusalem, a step the Council of Jerusalem would confirm (Acts 15). The point is not that the Law was bad, but that in Christ God gathers Jew and Gentile into one people (Ephesians 2:14). Every parish has people some would rather not sit at table with. Peter’s question still stands: who are we to hinder God?

r.h: I am the gate
set: Jesus is still speaking to the Pharisees who had questioned the man born blind and driven him out (9:34, 40–41). That man heard the voice of Jesus and followed him; those who should have been his shepherds cast him out. The background is Ezekiel 34, where God condemns shepherds who feed themselves and promises to shepherd his flock himself. In Palestine the sheep of several flocks were often kept at night in one walled fold with a gatekeeper; in the morning each shepherd called his own sheep out by his voice.
str: vv. 1–5: the figure: thief and shepherd, gate and voice.
v. 6: they do not understand.
vv. 7–10: “I am the gate”: salvation, pasture, abundant life.
kw: Not the usual word for parable (parabolē), which John never uses. It means a veiled saying whose sense opens to those who come to believe (compare 16:25, 29).
Jesus is both the gate (v. 7) and, a few verses later, the shepherd (v. 11). As the gate he is the only right way into the flock, for shepherds as well as sheep; as the shepherd he leads them.
The thief takes; Jesus gives more than enough, as at Cana and at the feeding of the five thousand, where more was left over than was needed (6:12–13).
vv: He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.

Faith in John is personal: Mary Magdalene will know the risen Lord when he calls her by name (20:16). “Leads them out” recalls the man born blind: driven out of the synagogue, he is found by Jesus (9:35).
I am the gate. Whoever enters by me will be saved, and will come in and go out and find pasture.

“Come in and go out” is a biblical way of describing a whole life lived in safety (compare Deuteronomy 28:6; Psalm 121:8). Christ is not a gate that shuts the sheep in, but one that gives them a home and wide pasture.
I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly.
The purpose of the whole Gospel in one line (compare 20:31).
ch: The Second Vatican Council begins its images of the Church with this passage: the Church is a sheepfold whose one and necessary door is Christ (Lumen Gentium 6; CCC 754). The image is both comfort and charge. For the faithful it means safety: no one who comes in by Christ is a stranger. For pastors it means that every ministry must enter by the same gate, serving a flock that belongs to Christ and not owning it.

qa: Who are the “thieves and bandits” who came before Jesus?

Not Moses and the prophets, whom Jesus honors (5:46). Most commentators think of false leaders and would-be messiahs who used the people for their own ends, and, in this context, of those who had just cast out the healed man. The warning applies in every age to anyone who leads God’s people without entering by Christ.
study: Whom do I find it hard to sit at table with? What would Peter’s question, “who was I that I could hinder God?”, mean for me?
Do I hear Christ calling me by name? Where is he leading me out to “find pasture” this week?

lead: Today the Church moves outward. Believers scattered by persecution reach Antioch, and some unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene speak of the Lord Jesus to Greeks; there the disciples are first called Christians. In the Temple at the feast of Dedication, Jesus says that no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand: “The Father and I are one.” Psalm 87 sees Zion as the mother city of all peoples, where even foreigners are counted as born.

r.h: First called Christians
set: Luke picks up a thread left at 8:4: the persecution after the death of Stephen scattered the believers, and they carried the word with them. Antioch on the Orontes, capital of the Roman province of Syria, was one of the largest cities of the empire, with a large Jewish community and many Gentiles drawn to the synagogue. Here, for the first time on a large scale, the Gospel is preached to Gentiles, and by ordinary believers whose names we are not told.
str: v. 19: the scattered believers speak to Jews only.
vv. 20–21: men of Cyprus and Cyrene speak to Greeks; many believe.
vv. 22–24: Jerusalem sends Barnabas; he sees grace and rejoices.
vv. 25–26: Barnabas brings Saul; a year of teaching; the name “Christians”.
kw: A real textual question. Many manuscripts read “Hellenists”, the word used in 6:1 for Greek-speaking Jews; others read “Greeks”. The contrast with v. 19 (“no one except Jews”) shows that Luke means Gentiles, and many translations, the Malayalam POC among them, say “Greeks”.

Barnabas’ name was explained as “son of encouragement” (4:36), and here he does what his name says: he “exhorted” (parekalei) them all to remain faithful. The man sent to inspect finds grace and encourages it.

A name formed like those given to the followers or household of a leader (compare “Herodians”, Mark 3:6). Many scholars think outsiders coined it. What others noticed about the disciples was that their life was about Christ.
vv: The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number became believers and turned to the Lord.
The preachers are nameless; the hand is the Lord’s. In Acts the growth of the Church is always first the Lord’s work.
When he came and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced,
A model for anyone sent to look at something new in the Church: look first for grace, and when you find it, rejoice.
it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called “Christians.”

Antioch became one of the great Churches of the ancient world. St Ignatius, its bishop early in the second century, is the first writer known to us who calls the Church “catholic” (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 8).
ch: The Church in Antioch shows what Easter does: persecution scatters, and the scattering becomes a sowing. The Church in Jerusalem does not shut down the new work; it sends a wise and generous man to strengthen it. Barnabas then goes to look for Saul, whom many still feared (9:26–27), and puts him to work. Much of the Church’s mission depends on people like Barnabas, who notice the gifts of others.

r.h: No one will snatch them out of my hand
