set: The feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) recalls the cleansing and rededication of the Temple by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC, after Antiochus IV had profaned it (1 Maccabees 4:36–59). It falls in December, so “It was winter”. Jesus walks in the portico of Solomon, the covered colonnade on the east side of the Temple court where the first believers would later gather (Acts 5:12). At the feast of the Temple’s consecration, Jesus will speak of himself as the one “whom the Father has sanctified and sent” (10:36).
str: vv. 22–24: the setting and the demand: “tell us plainly”.
vv. 25–26: works that testify, and unbelief.
vv. 27–29: the sheep hear, are known, follow, receive eternal life, and are held.
v. 30: “The Father and I are one.”
kw: The Greek name of the feast means “renewal” or “inauguration”. The Temple renewed by the Maccabees points to the new Temple, the body of Jesus (2:21).
The wolf “snatches” the sheep (10:12); no one can snatch them out of the hand of Jesus or of the Father. The believer’s security rests not on his own grip on God but on God’s grip on him.
Jesus does not say “one person” (masculine heis) but “one” in the neuter (hen): one in being and in work, while remaining Father and Son.
vv: How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.
“The Jews” here are the Temple authorities and those who sided with them, as often in John (compare 9:22); Jesus and his disciples were Jews too. Jesus answers that his works have already spoken.
My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me.
Three short sentences make a whole spiritual life: listening, being known, following.
The Father and I are one.

St Augustine notes that “one” answers Arius, who made the Son less than the Father, and “are” answers Sabellius, who made Father and Son a single person (in substance). The Church’s faith holds both: one God, and distinct Persons (CCC 253–254).
ch: The Church reads this Gospel in the Easter season because the risen Shepherd keeps his promise: no one can snatch his own from his hand, not even death. This assurance is not presumption; it is hope resting on the faithfulness of God (CCC 1821). The verse “The Father and I are one” became a key text in the fourth-century defense of the true divinity of the Son, whom the Creed confesses as “consubstantial with the Father”.

qa: Does “No one will snatch them out of my hand” mean that a believer can never be lost?

No power outside us can snatch us from Christ. What remains is our own ability to stop listening and following. So the Church speaks of final perseverance as a grace we hope for and ask for, trusting in God’s faithfulness (CCC 2016).
study: Like Barnabas, do I look first for the grace of God in what is new and unfamiliar in the Church? Whose gifts could I encourage?
Which of the three, hearing his voice, being known, following, is weakest in me now?

lead: The word of God “continued to advance”, and in Antioch the Holy Spirit speaks while the Church is at worship: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul”. Mission is born of liturgy and fasting. In the Gospel Jesus gives his last public summary: he has come as light, not to judge the world but to save it. Psalm 67 prays that God’s saving power be known among all nations. Today is the optional memorial of St Anselm, who wrote that he believed in order to understand.

r.h: Set apart for the work
set: Chapter 12 ends with the death of Herod Agrippa I and the growth of the word of God (12:23–24): persecutors pass, and the word remains. Barnabas and Saul had taken famine relief from Antioch to Jerusalem (11:29–30) and now return with John Mark. From here on Antioch, not Jerusalem, is the base of the mission to the nations, and Saul moves to the center of the story.
str: 12:24–25: the word grows; Barnabas and Saul return with John Mark.
13:1: five prophets and teachers.
13:2–3: the Spirit speaks at worship; fasting, prayer, laying on of hands.
13:4–5a: sent by the Spirit to Seleucia, Cyprus and Salamis.
kw: to worship, to serve in the liturgy
The word behind our “liturgy” (13:2). The Spirit speaks while the community is at worship and fasting. The great missionary journeys begin not from a planning meeting but from prayer.
Paul will use the same verb of himself: “set apart for the gospel of God” (Romans 1:1). To be set apart is not to be cut off from people but to be dedicated to a task for them.
member of the court, one brought up with

Manaen had been brought up with Herod Antipas, the tetrarch who beheaded John the Baptist. The list of leaders joins a Levite from Cyprus, Simeon called Niger (“black”), Lucius from Cyrene in Africa, a man of the royal court and a former persecutor. The Gospel had reached the palace and the street.
vv: Then after completing their mission Barnabas and Saul returned to Jerusalem

A known puzzle. The oldest manuscripts read “to Jerusalem”, but the story needs a return from Jerusalem to Antioch, and other manuscripts read “from Jerusalem”, as the Malayalam POC does. Some scholars read the Greek as “they returned, having completed their service in Jerusalem”.
While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said,
Luke does not say how the Spirit spoke; most likely through one of the prophets named in v. 1.
So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit,

The community laid hands on them and sent them (v. 3); Luke now says the Spirit sent them. This was not the first making of Saul an apostle, for his call came from the risen Lord (Galatians 1:1), but the Church’s blessing and sending for a particular work. The Spirit calls and the Church sends, and both are one act.
ch: The Church has always seen in this scene the pattern of mission: the initiative of the Spirit, the discernment of a community at prayer, and the sending by the Church with the laying on of hands. Pope St Paul VI wrote that evangelizing is the grace and vocation proper to the Church, her deepest identity (Evangelii Nuntiandi 14). A parish that prays and fasts together will sooner or later hear the same voice: set someone apart for the work.

r.h: I have come as light into the world
set: These verses close the first half of John’s Gospel, which many call the Book of Signs. The evangelist has just said that many did not believe, while some leaders believed in secret (12:37–43). Then, with no place or time given, Jesus “cried aloud” a last public summary of all he has said: to believe in him is to believe in the Father; he is light; he came to save; his word will judge. From chapter 13 on he speaks only to his own.
str: vv. 44–45: to believe in Jesus and to see him is to believe in and see the one who sent him.
v. 46: light in the darkness.
vv. 47–48: not to judge but to save; the word as judge.
vv. 49–50: the Father’s commandment is eternal life.
kw: Used of Jesus teaching in the Temple at the feast of Tabernacles (7:28, 37). A public, urgent cry, like a prophet’s; this is the last time Jesus addresses the crowds in John.
Not only the absence of light but the world closed against God (1:5). No one who believes need “remain” there: the verb suggests that all begin in the dark, and Christ comes to lead them out.
Jesus does not come as a judge looking for the guilty. Yet a word refused becomes a judgment: the light itself shows what a person has chosen (3:19).
vv: Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in him who sent me.
Jesus never draws people to himself apart from the Father. Faith in him is the way into the Father’s own life.
I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness.
The Easter candle, carried into the dark church at the Vigil with the chant “The Light of Christ”, proclaims this verse without words.
I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.
Compare 3:17. The Father’s purpose in sending the Son is mercy.
ch: The Church reads these verses as Jesus’ own summary of the Gospel. The Catechism teaches that Christ has full right to judge, yet he came to save, and that by rejecting grace in this life a person already judges himself (CCC 679). So the Church preaches with urgency and gentleness together: the light is offered to all, and no one is forced into it.

rite: St Anselm (1033–1109), born at Aosta, was a monk and abbot of Bec in Normandy and then Archbishop of Canterbury; he is a Doctor of the Church. In his Proslogion he prays: “I do not seek to understand in order to believe, but I believe in order to understand.” His watchword, faith seeking understanding, suits today’s Gospel: whoever believes does not remain in darkness, and faith becomes a light for the mind as well as the heart.
study: What does it mean for my parish that mission is born from worship and fasting, as in Antioch?
Where in my life am I still choosing to “remain in the darkness”? What would it take to step into the light?

lead: Paul’s first recorded sermon is preached in a synagogue, after the reading of the Law and the Prophets. He tells Israel’s story from Egypt to David and then names its fulfilment: “Of this man’s posterity God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised.” In the Gospel, just after the washing of the feet, Jesus tells the Twelve that whoever receives the one he sends receives him. Psalm 89 sings of God’s covenant with David, the thread that ties both readings together.

r.h: A word of exhortation
set: From Cyprus the missionaries sail to the south coast of Asia Minor and go inland to Antioch in Pisidia, a Roman colony, not to be confused with Antioch in Syria. Luke now calls Saul by his Roman name, Paul (13:9), and Paul takes the lead. John Mark goes back to Jerusalem; Luke gives no reason, but the departure will later divide Paul and Barnabas (15:37–39). The order of the synagogue service matches what we know from other sources: readings from the Law and the Prophets, then a word of teaching (compare Luke 4:16–21).
str: vv. 13–15: the journey to Antioch in Pisidia; the invitation after the readings.
vv. 16–22: God’s deeds from the exodus to David.
vv. 23–25: from David to Jesus, with John the Baptist as witness.
kw: The same phrase describes the Letter to the Hebrews (Hebrews 13:22). It seems to have been a name for a sermon after the readings, as the homily follows the readings at Mass.

Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel and attended the synagogue without becoming full converts, like Cornelius (10:2). Paul addresses them together with the Israelites (v. 16): the bridge by which the Gospel would reach the nations was already standing.
God has brought Israel “a Savior”, the title the angel gave at Bethlehem (Luke 2:11). Paul presents Jesus not as a break with Israel’s story but as its promised goal.
vv: I have found David, son of Jesse, to be a man after my heart, who will carry out all my wishes.

A weaving together of Scripture: Psalm 89:20 (“I have found my servant David”), 1 Samuel 13:14 (“a man after his own heart”) and Isaiah 44:28 (“he shall carry out all my purpose”). Paul preaches as a Jew formed by the Scriptures.
Of this man’s posterity God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised;
The center of the sermon. God keeps a promise across a thousand years.
I am not worthy to untie the thong of the sandals on his feet.
Untying sandals was a slave’s task. The last and greatest of the prophets places himself below even that service.
ch: The Church sees in Paul’s sermon a model of how the Old Testament is read in the light of Christ: Israel’s history is not set aside but fulfilled. The Second Vatican Council, following St Augustine, says that the New Testament is hidden in the Old and the Old is made manifest in the New (Dei Verbum 16). At Mass the homily stands where Paul’s “word of exhortation” stood: after the readings, opening them for today.

r.h: Whoever receives one whom I send
set: Jesus has just washed the feet of his disciples (13:1–15) and told them to do the same for one another. These verses draw out the meaning: the servant is not above the master, and blessing lies not in knowing but in doing. In the same breath Jesus speaks of the betrayer, and yet he ends with the dignity of those he sends.
str: vv. 16–17: servant and master; the blessing of doing.
v. 18: “The one who ate my bread”: Psalm 41.
v. 19: foretold so that they may believe “I am he”.
v. 20: receiving the one sent.
kw: The word in v. 16 translated “messengers” is apostolos, the only place it occurs in John’s Gospel. The Twelve hear their name and their place at the same moment: sent ones, no greater than the one who sends them.

Literally “I am”. In Isaiah God says “I am he” to show that he alone foretells and fulfils (Isaiah 43:10). Jesus speaks so that his Passion, when it comes, will reveal who he is rather than disprove it.
As in the Beatitudes. John has only two such beatitudes (13:17; 20:29). Here the blessing belongs not to knowing the example but to doing it.
vv: you are blessed if you do them.
Knowing about service is easy; the blessing is promised to those who wash feet.
The one who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.

From Psalm 41:9, the prayer of a man betrayed by a trusted friend. To eat someone’s bread was to be bound in friendship; lifting the heel pictures a kick, or turning one’s back. The betrayal comes from within the circle of the table.
whoever receives one whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.

A chain runs from the Father to the humblest messenger of the Gospel. Jewish teaching knew a similar principle about envoys, later written in the Mishnah: a man’s agent is like the man himself (Berakhot 5:5).
ch: The Church hears in v. 20 a foundation of apostolic ministry: Christ sends the apostles as the Father sent him (20:21), and whoever receives them receives him (CCC 858). The dignity of the minister is not his own; it is Christ’s, and so it calls first for humility, since the servant is not greater than the master. The betrayer at the table reminds the Church that even those closest to Christ must keep watch over their hearts.

study: Paul read Israel’s history as leading to Jesus. Can I tell the story of my own life in the same way, seeing where God kept his promises?
Whom has Christ sent into my life this week? How did I receive them?

lead: Paul’s sermon reaches its heart: “God raised him from the dead”, and so fulfilled what he had promised to the ancestors, as the second psalm says: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” The same psalm is today’s responsorial psalm. In the Gospel, on the night before he dies, Jesus calms troubled hearts: he goes to prepare a place, and he himself is the way there. Today is the optional memorial of St George, martyr, and of St Adalbert, bishop and martyr.

r.h: God raised him from the dead
set: Paul turns from history to the present: “to us the message of this salvation has been sent.” Like the apostles throughout Acts, he tells the Passion briefly and lays the weight on the Resurrection and its witnesses. He speaks to fellow Jews and God-fearers as brothers, and he describes the condemnation of Jesus in Jerusalem as an act done without understanding, which God turned into the fulfilment of the prophets (compare 3:17).
str: vv. 26–29: the word sent to us; the Passion according to the Scriptures.
vv. 30–31: God raised him; the witnesses from Galilee.
vv. 32–33: the good news: the promise fulfilled; Psalm 2.
kw: Literally “not knowing”. Peter said the same in Jerusalem (3:17). The New Testament treats this ignorance as a real fault in those responsible, yet one that leaves room for repentance, and it never extends the guilt to all Jews of that time or of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).

Paul says Jesus was taken down from the “tree”, the word of Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where one hanged on a tree is under a curse. Peter uses it too (5:30; 10:39), and Paul explains it in Galatians 3:13: Christ became a curse for us.

In Psalm 2 the king of David’s line is declared God’s son on the day he is enthroned. The apostles see that “today” in the Resurrection: Jesus, eternally the Son, is now enthroned in power as Son in his risen humanity (Romans 1:4).
vv: Because the residents of Jerusalem and their leaders did not recognize him or understand the words of the prophets that are read every sabbath, they fulfilled those words by condemning him.
The irony is deliberate: the very prophets read aloud every sabbath were fulfilled by those who did not grasp them. The Church adds that all sinners are the authors of Christ’s Passion (CCC 598).
But God raised him from the dead;
One short verse carries the whole sermon. The verses before it tell what people did; this one tells what God did.
and they are now his witnesses to the people.
Paul does not count himself among those who came up from Galilee. He rests his preaching on the witnesses of the Easter appearances, as he does in 1 Corinthians 15:3–8.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Resurrection fulfils the promises of the Old Testament and of Jesus himself, and it joins Psalm 2 to the Resurrection as Paul does here (CCC 652–653). Each Sunday the Church gathers as Paul’s hearers did, to hear the Scriptures read and to be told that they are fulfilled in the risen Christ.

r.h: I am the way, and the truth, and the life
set: The supper is over and Jesus has foretold Peter’s denial (13:38). Into the disciples’ fear he speaks the first words of his long farewell. These words are often read at funerals, and rightly; but they were first spoken to men who were about to see their Master arrested and killed.
str: v. 1: “Do not let your hearts be troubled”: faith in God and in Jesus.
vv. 2–3: the Father’s house, a place prepared, a promise to come again.
vv. 4–6: Thomas’ question; “I am the way”.
kw: The same verb was used of Jesus himself, troubled in spirit before the betrayal (13:21). He does not ask from them a calm he has never known; he has passed through trouble and speaks from beyond it.
From the verb menō, to remain, a favorite word of John. The Father and the Son will make their “home” (monē) with whoever loves Jesus (14:23). Heaven begins as an indwelling now.
Not only a road to walk but a Person to walk with. The first Christians were called people “of the Way” (Acts 9:2).
vv: In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places.

Many rooms: room enough for all, and each person known. Earlier in John “my Father’s house” was the Temple (2:16); now it is the Father’s own presence, to which the risen body of Jesus, the true Temple, leads.
Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?
Thomas asks what the others only think. His honest question draws out one of the greatest sayings in the Gospel: a doubt spoken to Jesus becomes a door.
I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
St Augustine puts it simply: walk by Christ the man and you come to Christ who is God; by him you go to him (in substance).
ch: The Church confesses with this verse that Christ is the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5). For troubled hearts the verse is first a comfort: the way home is not a set of directions but a Person who walks with us. The Easter season lets us hear it in the light of the empty tomb: he has gone ahead, and the place is ready.

qa: Does “No one comes to the Father except through me” mean that those who are not Christians cannot be saved?

All who are saved are saved through Christ. The Second Vatican Council teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, yet seek God with a sincere heart and, moved by grace, try to do his will as they know it through conscience, can attain eternal salvation (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). There is one way, and the grace of Christ reaches further than our knowledge of it. This is no reason to slacken the mission; it is the reason for it (CCC 848).
rite: St George, a soldier martyred probably at Lydda in Palestine early in the fourth century, is honored in East and West alike; the stories of the dragon came much later and teach in picture that faith overcomes evil. Many churches in Kerala bear his name. St Adalbert (Vojtěch), Bishop of Prague, was martyred in 997 while preaching to the Prussians near the Baltic coast. Both did what Paul describes today: they were witnesses of the risen Lord to the people, at the cost of their lives.
study: Which of my troubles do I need to bring to Jesus this week with Thomas’ honesty?
Where am I trying to reach the Father by my own road rather than walking with Christ, the Way?

lead: On the next sabbath almost the whole city comes to hear Paul. Opposition follows; Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles in the words of Isaiah, and the disciples, though driven out, are “filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit”. In the Gospel Philip asks, “Lord, show us the Father”, and Jesus answers, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” Psalm 98 sings that all the ends of the earth have seen the saving power of God. Today is the optional memorial of St Fidelis of Sigmaringen, priest and martyr.

r.h: A light for the Gentiles
set: Paul’s first sermon had moved many: “many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas” (13:43). A week later the crowd is so large that some of the synagogue’s members and leaders turn against the preachers. Luke’s phrase “the Jews” here means these opponents in one city, not the Jewish people; many of the first believers in Antioch were themselves Jews. The pattern runs through Acts: the word goes first to the synagogue, and then also to the Gentiles (compare Romans 1:16, “to the Jew first and also to the Greek”).
str: vv. 44–45: the whole city gathers; jealousy and contradiction.
vv. 46–47: “We are now turning to the Gentiles”; Isaiah 49:6.
vv. 48–49: the Gentiles rejoice; the word spreads.
vv. 50–52: persecution; dust shaken off; joy and the Spirit.
kw: The same word can mean zeal for God or jealousy. Here it is the sad side: a religious zeal that cannot bear to see others welcomed. It is a temptation for believers in every age.
The word for the apostles’ boldness, which Luke treats as a gift of the Spirit (4:29, 31). Paul and Barnabas do not lose their nerve when opposed; they speak more plainly.

“As many as had been destined for eternal life became believers.” Luke stresses that faith is God’s gift and initiative. The Church does not read this as if some were created for damnation: God predestines no one to hell (CCC 1037). God’s call and the human response work together.
vv: It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken first to you.

“Necessary” because of God’s plan and promise: Israel is the first heir of the word. Turning to the Gentiles in this city does not cancel that; in the very next town Paul goes first to the synagogue again (14:1).
I have set you to be a light for the Gentiles, so that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.
Isaiah 49:6, from the song of the Servant. Simeon applied it to the child Jesus (Luke 2:32); Paul applies it to the mission. The light is Christ’s, and his messengers carry it.
And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
The chapter ends not in defeat but in joy. Christian joy does not depend on success; it comes from the Spirit.
ch: The Church reads this passage as the shape of every mission: welcome and rejection, and both met with joy. The Second Vatican Council recalls that the Jews remain most dear to God for the sake of their fathers, for his gifts and call are irrevocable (Nostra Aetate 4; Romans 11:28–29). Paul’s shaking off of the dust, a gesture Jesus had given his disciples (Luke 9:5), is not a curse; it leaves the matter in God’s hands, a sign that the preachers have done their part.

r.h: Show us the Father
set: The conversation at the Last Supper continues. Thomas has asked about the way; now Philip, who once told Nathanael, “Come and see” (1:46), asks to see the Father. His request voices the deepest longing of the Old Testament, the prayer of Moses: “Show me your glory, I pray” (Exodus 33:18).
str: v. 7: to know Jesus is to know the Father.
vv. 8–11: Philip’s request; “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father”; the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father.
vv. 12–14: greater works; prayer in his name.
kw: A perfect tense: to have seen and still to see. In Jesus the Father is not glimpsed for a moment but shown to stay.

“I am in the Father and the Father is in me.” Because of their unity the Father is wholly in the Son and the Son wholly in the Father (CCC 255). What Jesus says and does is the Father’s own speaking and working.
To ask “in my name” is not to add a formula but to ask as one united with Jesus, for what he wills, so that the Father may be glorified.
vv: Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me?
A gentle reproach, not a dismissal. One can live close to Jesus for years and still have more of him to discover.
Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.
The center of the passage. Jesus is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15); the Catechism calls the Son the Father’s one, perfect and unsurpassable Word (CCC 65).
the one who believes in me will also do the works that I do and, in fact, will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.

Not greater in power but wider in reach: through the Spirit the Church carries the Gospel to the ends of the earth. St Augustine, commenting on this verse, says that to make a sinner righteous is a greater work than to create heaven and earth (in substance; see CCC 1994).
ch: The Church sees in Philip’s request the question of every human heart, and in Jesus’ answer the whole of Christian faith: God is not hidden behind Jesus; he is shown in him. Asking “in his name” is the new thing Jesus gives his disciples on this night (CCC 2614). The prayers of the Mass end “through Christ our Lord”: this is what asking in his name means.

rite: St Fidelis of Sigmaringen (1578–1622), a lawyer who became a Capuchin friar, preached in the Swiss region of the Grisons at a time of bitter conflict among Christians. He was killed at Seewis in 1622 and is honored as the first martyr of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, founded that same year. Like Paul in Antioch of Pisidia, he kept preaching where he was not welcome. The Church remembers him today in a spirit of reconciliation, praying for unity among all who bear the name of Christ.
study: When I meet opposition for my faith, what would it mean for me to be “filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit” rather than with resentment?
Philip had been with Jesus a long time. What have I not yet discovered about Jesus, and so about the Father?

lead: The Fifth Sunday of Easter turns from the appearances of the Risen Lord to the life of his body, the Church. Saul, the persecutor who has met the Lord, cannot get in through the door of the Jerusalem community until Barnabas takes him by the hand. John’s letter says that love is shown in deeds, and that whoever keeps the commandment abides in God. In the Gospel Jesus gives the image that holds it all together: the vine and the branches.

The word that runs through the letter and the Gospel is abide. The psalm is the last part of Psalm 22, the psalm whose opening cry Jesus prayed on the Cross. Here it ends in praise in the great assembly, with the ends of the earth turning to the Lord. The Church of Acts, growing in Judea, Galilee and Samaria, is the beginning of that answer.

r.h: Barnabas took him
set: Saul has met the Risen Lord on the road to Damascus (9:1–19), has preached in the synagogues there that Jesus is the Son of God (9:20), and has escaped a plot by being let down the city wall in a basket (9:23–25). Luke now brings him to Jerusalem. Paul’s own account in Galatians 1:17–19 adds that he first went away into Arabia, and that it was after three years that he went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas, staying fifteen days and seeing James the Lord’s brother. Luke tells it more briefly and keeps his eye on one thing: how the former persecutor was received.

Background. Barnabas first appears in 4:36–37: a Levite from Cyprus named Joseph, who sold a field and laid the money at the apostles’ feet. The apostles called him Barnabas, which Luke explains as “son of encouragement”. The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews in Jerusalem. Stephen had argued with members of their synagogues (6:9), and Saul had stood by at his death (7:58; 8:1). Now Saul takes Stephen’s place in the same debate and meets the same danger.
str: v. 26: Saul tries to join the disciples, and they are afraid of him.
v. 27: Barnabas brings him to the apostles and speaks for him.
vv. 28–29: Saul speaks boldly in Jerusalem and argues with the Hellenists, who try to kill him.
v. 30: the believers bring him down to Caesarea and send him to Tarsus.
v. 31: the Church has peace, is built up and grows.
¶ Verse 31 is one of Luke’s short summaries, like 2:42–47, 4:32–35 and 6:7. They are pauses in the story that show the whole Church at a glance.
kw: Used twice here (vv. 27, 28). The noun parrēsia means plain, fearless speech, the courage of the apostles before the council (4:13, 29, 31). The same noun is the “boldness before God” of today’s second reading (1 John 3:21).

The Church grows “in the comfort of the Holy Spirit” (v. 31). Luke explains the name Barnabas as “son of paraklēsis” (4:36). The word belongs to the same family as Paraclete, the name Jesus gives the Spirit in John. Barnabas does on earth what the Spirit does in the whole Church.

In the best manuscripts the word is singular: “the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria”. Later manuscripts have the plural, “churches”. The singular shows one Church spread over several regions.
vv: they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple.
Their fear was reasonable. He had dragged men and women off to prison (8:3). A conversion can be real and still need time before others can trust it.
But Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles,

Barnabas risks his own good name. He listens to Saul’s story and then tells it for him: the road, the Lord who spoke, the bold preaching in Damascus. Every parish needs someone who will take the newcomer by the hand.
they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

Caesarea was the Roman port on the coast. Tarsus in Cilicia was Saul’s home city (21:39). He disappears from the story for some years, until Barnabas goes to Tarsus to look for him and brings him to Antioch (11:25–26). Barnabas opens the door a second time.
Living in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it increased in numbers.
Two things that seem opposed stand together: fear of the Lord, which is reverence, and comfort. The Church’s growth here comes from the Spirit, not from strategy.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of faith in Jesus as the Son of God, recalls Paul’s encounter on the road to Damascus and his first preaching that Jesus is the Son of God (CCC 442). The Church honours Barnabas, whom Acts calls an apostle (14:14), with a memorial on 11 June. In him she sees the ministry of welcome and encouragement: the one who believed in another’s conversion before the others did. Saul’s story also shows that the Church is not a club of the deserving. It is the place where an enemy can become a brother.

r.h: In truth and action
set: The First Letter of John comes from the tradition of the beloved disciple and was probably written near the end of the first century. Ancient tradition ascribes it to the apostle John; the letter does not name its writer, and many scholars think it comes from a disciple within the circle of John. It speaks to communities shaken after some members had left them (2:19). Its two great concerns are true faith in Jesus who has come in the flesh (4:2) and real love for brothers and sisters.

Just before our passage, John says that we know love because Christ laid down his life for us, and asks how God’s love can abide in anyone who sees a brother or sister in need and refuses help (3:16–17). Today’s verses follow from that.
str: v. 18: love in deeds, not only in words.
vv. 19–20: a troubled heart, and God who is greater than our hearts.
vv. 21–22: boldness before God and prayer that is heard.
v. 23: one commandment with two sides: believe in the name of the Son, and love one another.
v. 24: abiding in God, and the Spirit as the sign.
kw: For John, truth is not only correct words. It is what is real, and it comes from God. To love “in truth” is to love in a way that is real, and to be “from the truth” (v. 19) is to belong to God.
Confidence before God, the openness of a child who can speak to a father without fear (v. 21). The same word describes the apostles’ bold speech in Acts.

One of John’s favourite words, here in v. 24 and again and again in today’s Gospel passage. It means to stay, to dwell, to make one’s home. Christian life is not a visit to God but a remaining with him.
vv: Little children, let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action.
“Little children” is the tender address of an old teacher. The verse does not despise words; it asks that they be true, and true words become deeds.
whenever our hearts condemn us; for God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.

The verse is a comfort. Our own heart can accuse us too much, or too little. God’s knowledge is larger than our self-condemnation, and his mercy is larger still. The Catechism quotes these words when it speaks of God’s holiness and mercy (CCC 208), and again when it speaks of conscience (CCC 1781).
And this is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another,
The commandment is singular, yet it has two sides. Faith and love are not two separate tasks. Faith in the Son who loved us becomes love for one another.
And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit that he has given us.
The first mention of the Spirit in the letter. The sign that God dwells in us is not a feeling of our own making but a gift we have received.
ch: St Augustine preached ten homilies on this letter during Easter time. In one of them he gives the famous saying “Love, and do what you will”, meaning that if the root within is love, nothing but good can come from it (in substance). He did not mean that anything goes. He meant that love is the root from which every good act must grow, which is exactly the teaching of v. 18. The Church reads this letter in the Easter season because it shows what the new life of Easter looks like day by day: faith in the Son, love that acts, and the Spirit abiding within.

r.h: I am the vine, you are the branches
set: We are at the Last Supper, in the long farewell discourse of John 13–17. At the end of chapter 14 Jesus says, “Rise, let us be on our way” (14:31), and yet the discourse continues. Many scholars think chapters 15–17 were added to the first discourse as the Gospel took shape; others think the words were spoken on the way. Either way, the Church receives them as the Lord’s farewell teaching.

Background. In the Old Testament Israel is God’s vine, planted with love and tended with care, yet often disappointing: Isaiah 5:1–7, Psalm 80:8–16, Jeremiah 2:21. The Jewish historian Josephus describes a great golden vine over the entrance of the Temple sanctuary. When Jesus says “I am the true vine”, he presents himself as the faithful Israel in person, and his disciples belong to God’s people by belonging to him. This is the last of the seven “I am” sayings in John with an image: bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, and vine.
str: vv. 1–3: the vine, the vinegrower and the pruning; the disciples already cleansed by the word.
vv. 4–5: “Abide in me”: the branch lives only on the vine.
v. 6: the branch that does not abide.
vv. 7–8: prayer that is answered, much fruit, and the Father glorified.
kw: “True” in John means real, the genuine thing of which others were signs, as in “the true light” (1:9) and “the true bread from heaven” (6:32).

A play on words in the Greek. The Father “prunes” (kathairei, v. 2) the fruitful branch, and the disciples are already “cleansed” (katharoi, v. 3) by the word. Pruning and cleansing are the same action of love.
The key word of the passage, repeated again and again in vv. 4–7. It is not an effort to cling but a staying put: in his word, in his love, in his sacraments, in his Church.
vv: I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinegrower.
The Father is not far away. He is the one with his hands in the soil, looking after every branch.
Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.
Any farmer in Kerala knows that a plant cut back grows stronger. Pruning hurts, but it is a sign that the vinegrower expects more fruit, not a sign of his anger.
I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
St Augustine notes that the Lord did not say “without me you can do little”, but “nothing” (in substance). The branch does not produce the sap; it receives it.
Whoever does not abide in me is thrown away like a branch and withers;

Vine wood is useless for building; Ezekiel says that no peg can be made of it (Ezekiel 15:2–5). Augustine says that the branch has only two places to be, either in the vine or in the fire (in substance).
My Father is glorified by this, that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.
The fruit is not success in the world’s sense. It is the life of a disciple. Even at the end of the Gospel, being a disciple is still something we “become”.
ch: The Second Vatican Council lists the vine among the images of the Church: Christ is the true vine who gives life and fruitfulness to the branches, that is, to us, who through the Church abide in him (Lumen Gentium 6). The Catechism quotes vv. 4–5 to describe the intimate communion between Christ and those who follow him (CCC 787), and it explains that the fruit spoken of here is the holiness of a life made fruitful by union with Christ (CCC 2074). The Church has always heard in the vine a hint of the Eucharist too: the cup of the fruit of the vine which becomes his blood is the sap that runs through the branches.

qa: Does “apart from me you can do nothing” mean that our efforts do not matter?

No. It means that even our good efforts are a gift. The Catechism teaches that God’s grace comes first and prepares us, and that God’s initiative calls for our own real response (CCC 2001–2002). The branch truly bears the fruit, but only because the sap of the vine is running in it.
Is verse 6 about hell?

It is a serious warning. To cut oneself off from Christ ends in loss, and the Church teaches that a person who dies refusing God’s love by mortal sin remains separated from him for ever (CCC 1033). But the verse names no one. It is spoken to disciples so that they may abide. While we live, the way back to the vine is always open through repentance and the sacrament of reconciliation.
Why were the disciples so slow to receive Saul?

Because they had suffered from him. Fear after real harm is not a sin. What Acts shows is the way through it: someone who knew both sides, Barnabas, took the risk of trust and spoke for him. Communities today face the same task when someone who once did harm comes back changed.
rite: In the Easter season the Paschal candle stands near the ambo or the altar until Pentecost, a sign that the Risen Lord is present among us. At the preparation of the gifts the priest blesses God for the wine, “fruit of the vine and work of human hands”, which will become our spiritual drink: the vine of today’s Gospel comes to the altar. In Year B every Sunday of Easter except the Third takes its Gospel from John, and on Wednesday this week the Mass will read the same passage of the vine again. At home, the Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus until Pentecost.
study: Who is the Saul in my parish or family, the person others are slow to trust? Could I be a Barnabas for him or her?
John asks for love “in truth and action”. Which kind words of mine need to become a deed this week?
What pruning has God done in my life, and what fruit has come of it?
How do I abide in the vine: in prayer, in the Word, in the Eucharist, in the community? Which of these is weakest in me now?

lead: At Lystra a crowd takes two missionaries for gods, and Paul and Barnabas rush in among the people to stop the sacrifice. In the Gospel Jesus promises that the Father and he will come and make their home with those who love him, and that the Holy Spirit will teach and remind. Psalm 115 answers both: glory belongs not to us but to the Lord’s name, and the idols of silver and gold are only the work of human hands.

r.h: We are mortals just like you
set: This is the first missionary journey of Paul and Barnabas (chapters 13–14), sent out by the church of Antioch in Syria (13:1–3). After Pisidian Antioch and Iconium, a threat of stoning drives them on to Lystra and Derbe, towns of Lycaonia in the south of present-day Turkey. Augustus had made Lystra a Roman colony, but the ordinary people spoke their own Lycaonian language.

Background. The Roman poet Ovid tells an old tale of Jupiter and Mercury (Zeus and Hermes, in Greek) visiting the neighbouring region of Phrygia in human form, unrecognised by everyone except one old couple. Many commentators think a local story of this kind explains why the crowd was so quick to see gods in the two strangers.
str: vv. 5–7: the plot at Iconium and the flight to Lystra and Derbe.
vv. 8–10: a man lame from birth is healed.
vv. 11–13: the crowd cries out that the gods have come; the priest of Zeus prepares a sacrifice.
vv. 14–18: Barnabas and Paul tear their clothes and speak of the living God.
kw: The crowd shouts in its local tongue, which Paul and Barnabas probably did not understand. This may be why they react only when the oxen and garlands arrive (v. 14).
Empty, vain things. The Greek Old Testament uses this kind of word for idols. Paul calls the people away from what cannot give life to the God who does.
“Mortals just like you” (v. 15): people with the same weakness. James 5:17 uses the same word of Elijah. The apostles will not let a miracle make them more than human.
vv: And Paul, looking at him intently and seeing that he had faith to be healed,
Luke tells this healing much like Peter’s healing of the man lame from birth at the Temple gate, where Peter too “looked intently” at him (3:4). The same Lord works through both apostles.
“Stand upright on your feet.” And the man sprang up and began to walk.
No name is invoked aloud here, but the sermon he had just heard was about Jesus. Faith came by hearing, and healing followed.
We are mortals just like you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God,
Tearing one’s clothes was a Jewish sign of horror at blasphemy. The greatest danger for a preacher is to be worshipped. Paul and Barnabas turn every eye away from themselves.
yet he has not left himself without a witness in doing good
To people who did not know the Scriptures, Paul begins with rain, harvest, food and joy. Creation itself speaks of the Creator.
ch: This is the first speech in Acts to a purely pagan audience, and it begins not from the prophets but from creation, as Paul will do again in Athens (17:22–31). The Church teaches that God can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason (CCC 36, from the First Vatican Council). She rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions (Nostra Aetate 2), and like Paul and Barnabas she will never let a creature, however gifted, take the place of the living God.

r.h: We will make our home with them
set: We are at the Last Supper. One after another the disciples interrupt with questions: Peter (13:36), Thomas (14:5), Philip (14:8), and now Judas, “not Iscariot”. Luke calls him Judas son of James (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13), and tradition identifies him with Thaddeus (Mark 3:18). The Church honours him with St Simon on 28 October.
str: v. 21: love is proved by keeping his commandments, and he will reveal himself.
v. 22: Judas asks why to them and not to the world.
vv. 23–24: the answer: the Father and the Son will come and dwell.
vv. 25–26: the Advocate will teach and remind.
kw: The same word as the “dwelling places” of the Father’s house in 14:2. There, we go to dwell with God; here, God comes to dwell with us. The Father’s house begins now in the heart that loves.
Literally one called to stand beside someone: a helper, a defender, a comforter. In 1 John 2:1 the same word is used of Jesus himself; in John 14:16 the Spirit is “another Advocate”.
The Spirit will bring back to mind all that Jesus said. The Gospels themselves are fruit of this remembering.
vv: Lord, how is it that you will reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?
Judas perhaps expected a public triumph. Jesus answers by speaking of love, not of display.
Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.
Not a passing visit but a home. The whole Trinity dwells in the one who loves: the Father, the Son, and, as the next verses say, the Spirit.
will teach you everything, and remind you of all that I have said to you.
The Spirit does not bring a new Gospel. He makes the one Gospel understood and alive in every age.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 23 when it says that the goal of God’s whole plan is that his creatures enter the perfect unity of the Blessed Trinity, who already now come to dwell in us (CCC 260). It explains that Paraclete means “he who is called to one’s side” (CCC 692), and it calls the Holy Spirit the Church’s living memory (CCC 1099).

qa: Why did the Risen Jesus not show himself to the whole world?

In Acts Peter says that God allowed him to appear not to all the people but to witnesses chosen beforehand (Acts 10:40–41). God does not force himself on anyone. He shows himself to those who love and keep his word, and through their witness he reaches the world.
study: Where am I tempted to take credit for what God has done, as the crowd at Lystra wanted to give it to Paul and Barnabas?
If the Father and the Son make their home in me, what in my daily life would I want to tidy, and what would I want to open?

lead: Paul is stoned and left for dead at Lystra, gets up, and goes on. The journey ends where it began, at Antioch, with a report: God had opened a door of faith for the Gentiles. In the Gospel Jesus leaves his peace with men who are about to be badly shaken. Psalm 145 lets the friends of the Lord speak of the glory of his kingdom, the kingdom that Paul says we enter through many persecutions.

r.h: A door of faith for the Gentiles
set: The crowd that wanted to worship Paul yesterday is turned against him today. Opponents from Antioch of Pisidia and Iconium, where Paul had already met resistance, arrive and stir up the people. Luke means particular opponents from those cities; at Iconium a great number of Jews had in fact believed (14:1). Paul himself later recalls, “Once I received a stoning” (2 Corinthians 11:25), and 2 Timothy 3:11 recalls his sufferings at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra. Timothy came from Lystra (16:1).

After Derbe the apostles do not take the short road home through Tarsus. They go back the way they came, through the very towns that had driven them out, to strengthen the new believers. Then they sail home to Antioch in Syria, the church that had sent them out (13:1–3).
str: vv. 19–20: Paul is stoned, rises, and goes to Derbe.
vv. 21–23: the return journey: strengthening, encouraging, appointing elders.
vv. 24–26: the way back to Antioch.
vv. 27–28: the report to the church.
kw: Literally pressure, being pressed hard. Paul does not promise new Christians an easy road (v. 22). Suffering is not a sign that God has failed; it is part of the way into his kingdom.
Originally to stretch out the hand, as in voting; then simply to appoint. The apostles leave behind a recognised ministry in each church, with prayer and fasting (v. 23).
God opened it; the apostles only walked through it. Paul uses the same picture of an open door for the Gospel (1 Corinthians 16:9).
vv: Then they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead.
Saul once guarded the coats of those who stoned Stephen (7:58). Now he knows the stones himself.
“It is through many persecutions that we must enter the kingdom of God.”
This is not gloom. It is honest care for new believers, said by a man still bruised from Lystra. They will not be surprised when trouble comes.
And after they had appointed elders for them in each church, with prayer and fasting they entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had come to believe.

The ministry of the Church was still taking shape, and the titles were not yet fixed as they are today. What is clear already is that the apostles did not leave communities without shepherds, and that they handed them over not to themselves but to the Lord.
how he had opened a door of faith for the Gentiles.
The report is about what God has done, not about the missionaries’ hardships. This verse prepares tomorrow’s question: on what terms do the Gentiles come in?
ch: Pope Benedict XVI took the title of his letter announcing the Year of Faith, Porta Fidei (2011), from this verse: the door of faith is always open for us. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the apostles took care to appoint successors so that the mission entrusted to them would continue (Lumen Gentium 20). Paul’s return to the towns that had stoned him shows the heart of a shepherd: the new believers mattered more to him than his own safety.

r.h: My peace I give to you
set: The Last Supper discourse continues. Peace, shalom, was the ordinary greeting and farewell among Jews. Jesus takes the everyday word and fills it: his peace is the wholeness that comes from God, and he gives it on the night he is to be betrayed. After the resurrection his first word to the disciples will be “Peace be with you” (20:19).
str: v. 27: the gift of peace; do not be troubled.
v. 28: “I am going to the Father”.
v. 29: he tells them beforehand so that they may believe.
vv. 30–31a: the ruler of this world has no power over him; he does what the Father commands.
kw: The Greek word carries the Hebrew shalom: not only the absence of war but wholeness, harmony with God and others.
Used of water stirred up. John uses it of Jesus himself, troubled at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33) and at the approach of his hour (12:27; 13:21). He who was troubled for us gives us his peace.
John’s name for the devil (12:31; 16:11). He is coming in the betrayal and the arrest, but he has no hold on Jesus, who goes to the Cross out of love and obedience.
vv: I do not give to you as the world gives.
The world’s peace often depends on circumstances, or on keeping trouble away. His peace remains even in trouble, because it comes from him.
because the Father is greater than I.
See the question below. Jesus wants the disciples to rejoice that he is going home to the Father, not to cling to him for themselves.
He has no power over me;
Literally “in me he has nothing”. There is nothing in Jesus that belongs to the evil one. His death will not be a defeat but an offering.
ch: In the Roman Mass, before the sign of peace, the priest prays: “Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your Apostles: Peace I leave you, my peace I give you”. So this verse is heard at every Mass, and the peace we give one another flows from the Lord’s own gift, not from our feelings. St Augustine teaches that the Father is greater than the Son in the “form of a servant” that the Son took, while in the form of God the Son is equal to the Father (in substance).

qa: If Jesus is God, how can he say “the Father is greater than I”?

The Church confesses the Son as one in being with the Father. Fathers such as St Augustine read this verse of the Son’s human nature: as man, he is less than the Father. Others also saw in it the Father as the source from whom the Son eternally receives all that he is, without being any less God. Either way, the verse speaks of the Son’s love and obedience, not of a lesser divinity.
study: When trouble comes, do I take it as a sign that God has abandoned me, or as part of the road Paul spoke of?
Next time I give the sign of peace at Mass, whom do I most need to give it to in my heart?

lead: A hard question reaches the young Church: must Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses in order to be saved? Antioch does not settle it alone. It sends Paul and Barnabas up to Jerusalem, to the apostles and the elders. The Gospel repeats Sunday’s passage of the vine and the branches, and today it is heard beside a Church learning how to stay one. Psalm 122 is a pilgrim song of going up to Jerusalem, the city built to be bound firmly together. Today the Church also remembers St Peter Chanel, martyr, and St Louis Grignion de Montfort, priest.

r.h: They went up to Jerusalem
set: Since Peter baptised the Roman centurion Cornelius and his household (chapters 10–11), Gentiles had been entering the Church. At Antioch Jews and Gentiles believed and ate together. Now some believers from Judea teach that Gentiles must first be circumcised. The apostles’ letter will later say that these men had no instructions from them (15:24).

The question was not foolish. Circumcision was the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:10–14), and the Law was Israel’s treasured gift. The believers from the party of the Pharisees (v. 5) were taking God’s covenant seriously; Paul himself had been a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). Many scholars connect this meeting with the visit to Jerusalem Paul describes in Galatians 2:1–10, while others think that was an earlier visit. It is usually dated around AD 49.
str: vv. 1–2: teachers from Judea at Antioch; sharp debate; Paul and Barnabas are sent to Jerusalem.
v. 3: on the way through Phoenicia and Samaria they bring great joy.
vv. 4–5: welcome in Jerusalem; some believers from the Pharisees insist on circumcision.
v. 6: the apostles and the elders meet.
kw: The covenant sign given to Abraham. The question was whether Gentiles who believed in Israel’s Messiah had to become Jews first.
Leaders of the Jerusalem church who now appear beside the apostles (11:30). The word gives us the English “priest” through the Latin presbyter.
Literally a matter to be searched out. The Church does not pretend the question is easy; she gathers to seek the answer together.
vv: Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.
The issue is not a custom but salvation itself. That is why it could not be left to each local church.
Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them,
Luke does not hide that the first Christians quarrelled. What matters is what they did with the quarrel: they took it to the apostles.
they reported the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the believers.
On the road to a difficult meeting they tell good news. The joy of the believers in Phoenicia and Samaria is already part of the answer.
The apostles and the elders met together to consider this matter.
A Church that listens, debates and decides together under the apostles. The pattern of every later council is here.
ch: The Church has long seen in this assembly at Jerusalem the pattern of her councils: the bishops, with Peter, gather, listen to what God has done, consider the Scriptures, and decide. The disagreement was real and was not resolved by one side shouting louder, but by coming together in the Spirit. Disputes in parishes and families can learn from this road: neither silence nor division, but going up together to seek the truth.

r.h: The Father, the vinegrower
set: The passage was read on Sunday; today the weekday Lectionary reaches it in its course through John. Heard after the first reading, it has a fresh note. The branches at Antioch and Jerusalem were very different, Jew and Gentile, and yet there is one vine. Unity does not come from making all branches alike but from all abiding in Christ.
str: vv. 1–3: Christ the vine, the Father the vinegrower, the word that cleanses.
vv. 4–6: abiding, or withering.
vv. 7–8: his words abiding in us, and the Father glorified.
kw: One who works the earth. The Father does not stand at a distance; he labours patiently over the vine.
The disciples are cleansed “by the word” (v. 3), and his “words” are to abide in them (v. 7). Abiding in Christ includes keeping his words in the heart.
In John the Father is glorified in the Son’s Passion and resurrection (13:31–32). Here he is glorified also in the fruit of the disciples.
vv: You have already been cleansed by the word that I have spoken to you.
Said after the washing of the feet (13:10). Every time we listen to his word with faith, the vinegrower is at work in us.
If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask for whatever you wish,
This is not a blank cheque. One whose heart is filled with his words learns to ask for what Christ wants, and such prayer is heard.
My Father is glorified by this, that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.
The Father’s glory is not taken from us. It shines when we become fully alive as disciples.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of the Holy Spirit in the liturgy, says that the Spirit is like the sap of the Father’s vine which bears fruit on its branches (CCC 1108). At the Jerusalem assembly the same Spirit kept the branches on the one vine, and at every Mass he gathers into one body people of every origin.

rite: St Peter Chanel was a French priest of the Society of Mary (the Marists) who went as a missionary to the island of Futuna in the Pacific. He was killed there on 28 April 1841, the first martyr of Oceania, and soon after his death the island became Christian. St Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort (died 28 April 1716) was a French priest who preached parish missions among the poor and wrote True Devotion to the Blessed Virgin, teaching that we go to Jesus through Mary. Both are optional memorials in the Roman calendar. Each in his own way abided in the vine and bore fruit beyond his own lifetime.
study: When there is disagreement in my family or parish, do I go silent, walk away, or seek the truth together with others?
What is one word of Jesus I want to abide in me this week?

lead: At the assembly in Jerusalem Peter speaks of grace, Barnabas and Paul tell what God has done among the Gentiles, and James, reading the prophet Amos, proposes the way forward. In the Gospel Jesus says, “Abide in my love”, and gives the reason for all his words: that his joy may be in us and our joy be complete. Psalm 96 calls on every nation to sing to the Lord. Today the Church keeps the memorial of St Catherine of Siena, virgin and Doctor of the Church.

r.h: No distinction between them and us
set: This is Peter’s last appearance in Acts. He recalls his own experience at the house of Cornelius, when the Holy Spirit fell on Gentiles before they were baptised (10:44–48). After Barnabas and Paul have spoken, James replies. This is James “the Lord’s brother” (Galatians 1:19), the leader of the church in Jerusalem (12:17; 21:18), respected for his faithfulness to the Law. His word therefore carries great weight with the believers from the Pharisees.

James quotes Amos 9:11–12 in the Greek form of the Old Testament, which speaks of other peoples seeking the Lord; the Hebrew text speaks of possessing the remnant of Edom. The four things the Gentiles are asked to avoid (v. 20) are, many scholars think, drawn from the rules that Leviticus 17–18 laid down for foreigners living among Israel.
str: vv. 7–11: Peter: God gave the Gentiles the Spirit; all are saved by grace.
v. 12: Barnabas and Paul tell of signs and wonders.
vv. 13–18: James: the prophets agree.
vv. 19–21: James proposes not to trouble the Gentiles, but to ask four things of them.
kw: In 11:12 the Spirit told Peter to go to Cornelius “not to make a distinction”. Now he says God himself made no distinction (v. 9).
God’s unearned favour. Peter’s conclusion (v. 11) is the heart of the matter: Jew and Gentile are saved in the same way, through the grace of the Lord Jesus.

Literally David’s tent or booth, fallen into ruin. James sees it rebuilt in the risen Son of David, and the Gentiles coming to seek the Lord there. The Gentiles join the restored house of Israel; they do not replace it.
vv: And God, who knows the human heart, testified to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us;
Peter’s argument is not a theory but an event. God had already decided, and the Church must follow.
and in cleansing their hearts by faith he has made no distinction between them and us.
The real cleanness God seeks is in the heart.
we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.
Notice the surprise: not “they will be saved as we are”, but “we will be saved as they are”. All stand before God in the same need of grace.
we should not trouble those Gentiles who are turning to God,
James listens before he speaks. His proposal protects the Gentiles from burdens and also protects the table fellowship of Jewish and Gentile believers.
ch: On the “yoke” of v. 10: Israel loved the Law as a gift, and Jewish tradition speaks gladly of taking on the yoke of the commandments. Peter is not mocking the Law. His point is that no one is saved by keeping it perfectly, but all are saved by grace. The Catechism teaches that our justification comes from the grace of God (CCC 1996). Verse 21 shows James’s respect for the synagogue where Moses is read every sabbath. The assembly found a way to keep both truths: salvation by grace for all, and charity toward the Jewish believers.

r.h: Abide in my love
set: These three verses come straight after the vine. The image now becomes plain speech: to abide in the vine is to abide in his love. There is a chain of love: the Father loves the Son, the Son loves the disciples, and the disciples are to remain in that love.
str: v. 9: as the Father has loved me, so I have loved you.
v. 10: keeping the commandments is the way of abiding.
v. 11: the purpose: his joy in us, our joy complete.
kw: The self-giving love of God. Here it flows from the Father, through the Son, to us.
Joy appears often in the farewell discourse (15:11; 16:20–24; 17:13). It is spoken on the night before the Passion, so it is a joy that suffering cannot take away (16:22).
“That your joy may be complete”, filled to the brim. John uses a similar phrase in his first letter (1 John 1:4).
vv: As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love.
We are loved with the very love that the Father has for the Son. We do not have to earn a place; we are asked to stay.
If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love,
Obedience is not the price of love but the way to stay in it, as Jesus himself stays in the Father’s love by doing his will.
so that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be complete.
The commandments are given for joy. A saint is a person whose joy has been made complete.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it teaches that charity, the fruit of the Spirit and fullness of the Law, keeps the commandments of God and of Christ (CCC 1824). Christian moral life is not a list of rules but remaining in a love that comes first from God.

qa: Why are Christians not bound by circumcision and the food laws of Moses?

Because the apostles, guided by the Spirit, recognised that Gentiles are saved by the grace of Christ without becoming Jews first. This does not mean that the Law was bad or that God has rejected Israel; God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). The moral teaching of the Law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains for all.
rite: St Catherine of Siena (1347–1380) was one of the youngest children of a large family of a dyer in Siena. She joined the lay Dominican women known as the Mantellate, lived a life of prayer and penance in her own home, nursed the sick and the plague-stricken, and gathered disciples. Though she had little formal schooling, she dictated many letters and her book, the Dialogue. She urged Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome, which he did in 1377, and she worked for peace and unity in a divided Church. She died in Rome on 29 April 1380, aged about thirty-three. St Paul VI declared her a Doctor of the Church in 1970, and St John Paul II named her a co-patroness of Europe in 1999. Like the assembly in Acts, she loved the Church enough to speak the truth to it, and she abided in the love of Christ, which today’s Gospel commands.
study: Peter says that “we will be saved … just as they will”. Do I secretly think that I deserve God’s grace more than others?
St Catherine spoke the truth to the Church out of love. Is there a truth I need to say with love, and a love I need to keep while saying it?

lead: The decision of Jerusalem goes out as a letter, carried by trusted men, and when it is read at Antioch the believers rejoice. The letter speaks a sentence the Church has made her own: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us”. In the Gospel Jesus gives his commandment of love, calls his disciples friends, and tells them, “You did not choose me but I chose you”. Psalm 57 gives thanks among the peoples. Today the Church also remembers St Pius V, pope.

r.h: It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us
set: The assembly chooses two leaders to go with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas. Both are prophets (15:32). Silas will soon become Paul’s companion on his second journey (15:40). He is usually identified with the Silvanus named in Paul’s letters (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Corinthians 1:19). The letter is addressed to Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia, the region where the trouble began.
str: v. 22: the choice of messengers.
vv. 23–29: the letter: greeting, disowning of the troublemakers, praise of Barnabas and Paul, the decision.
vv. 30–31: the letter is read at Antioch, and the believers rejoice.

¶ A note on the text: some ancient manuscripts, chiefly the so-called Western text, give the decree in a different form, without “what is strangled” and with the saying not to do to others what one would not want done to oneself.
kw: The usual word for the decision of an assembly. The Church joins the Holy Spirit to her own judgment: “to the Holy Spirit and to us”.
Only a few necessary things are asked. The apostles lay on the Gentiles no heavier burden than charity and the life of the community require.
The letter is received as paraklēsis (v. 31). The decision of the Church comes not as a weight but as comfort.
vv: though with no instructions from us,
The apostles make clear that the men who caused the trouble did not speak for them. Authority in the Church includes honestly correcting what was said in its name.
who have risked their lives for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ.
High praise for Barnabas and Paul. The Jerusalem church stands publicly behind the missionaries.
For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose on you no further burden than these essentials:
The Holy Spirit is named first. The apostles do not claim to have invented the decision; they have discerned it.
When its members read it, they rejoiced at the exhortation.
A dispute that began with dissension ends with joy. Truth spoken in charity unites.
ch: The Church has often echoed this formula, and it expresses the faith that the Holy Spirit guides the Church’s shepherds when they decide together with Peter. The episode shows how authority serves peace: the decision was reached together, sent with living witnesses, written with respect, and received with joy.

r.h: I have called you friends
set: The farewell discourse continues. The commandment of love was first given after the washing of the feet (13:34). Here it is repeated at the beginning and end of the passage (vv. 12, 17), which frames everything in between.
str: v. 12: love one another as I have loved you.
v. 13: the greatest love: to lay down one’s life.
vv. 14–15: no longer servants but friends.
vv. 16–17: chosen and appointed to bear lasting fruit; love one another.
kw: A friend shares what he knows. The disciples are friends because the Son has made known to them all that he heard from the Father (v. 15).
The same expression as the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (10:11).
The initiative is his. Disciples did not apply for the post; they were chosen and sent.
vv: No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.
He speaks of his own death the next day. And Paul will add that Christ died for us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8): he makes friends of those for whom he dies.
but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.
Friendship with God was said of Abraham (Isaiah 41:8) and Moses, who spoke with God face to face, as one speaks to a friend (Exodus 33:11). Now it is given to all disciples.
You did not choose me but I chose you.
Grace comes first. Our choice of him is always an answer to his choice of us.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the New Law is a law of love which lets us pass from the condition of a servant who does not know what his master is doing to that of a friend of Christ (CCC 1972). It also sees in v. 13 the love with which Jesus willingly offered his life (CCC 609).

rite: St Pius V (1504–1572) was a Dominican friar, Michele Ghislieri, who became pope in 1566. He put into effect the reforms of the Council of Trent, publishing the Roman Catechism, the reformed Breviary and the Roman Missal of 1570. He called Christians to pray the Rosary for the victory at Lepanto in 1571, and from this came the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary on 7 October. His optional memorial falls on 30 April. Like the apostles in today’s first reading, he served the unity of the Church by giving clear teaching for the life of the faithful.
study: Jesus calls me a friend. How would my prayer change if I spoke to him as a friend speaks to a friend?
Is there a decision of the Church that I find hard? Have I tried to read it, as the Antioch believers did, as encouragement rather than as burden?
